The expectation averages over predicted futures. This form makes the two roles explicit: learned dynamics predicts what an action may cause, whereas teaching determines which consequence is desirable. Optimizing bAt leaves the neural parameters θ unchanged. Unknown dynamics changes which candidate trajectories are credible. One response is to infer dynamics context from recent transitions and evaluate actions with context-conditioned world model, as in DOMINO [19]. Another is to condition trajectory generation on those transitions and use reward and dynamics guidance during sampling, as in MetaDiffuser [20]. Both specialize prediction through new evidence while leaving the learned parameters fixed. Their difference is where feasibility and preference enter the computation: in evaluation of candidates or in their generation and refinement. Online fitting offers complementary response to uncertain dynamics. MetaPusher updates meta-learned pushing model from task transitions and repairs its planning tree as predictions change [368]. SandwichResiduals instead fits small corrections around frozen predictor using latent prediction error [367]. Both adapt neural parameters at deployment. Their comparison with contextual prediction therefore turns on what changes: model parameters or the evidence supplied to an unchanged model. From goal-reaching to demonstration-conditioned futures. Latent planning supplied an early way to connect an intended state to control. Universal Planning Networks learned differentiable planner that optimizes candidate action sequence [179]. The optimized variables are actions, so this search can run with unchanged model weights. Demonstration-conditioned prediction adds preceding inference problem: determine which state evolution the new example calls for, rather than assume that the goal is already supplied. This inference can remain in latent space. OSVI-WM predicts demonstration-conditioned latent states and decodes them into attributed waypoints [21]. Demo-JEPA instead passes predicted latent goal to cross-entropy-method planner, retaining that goal until an achievement threshold permits progression [22]. Both combine world-model-based control with an explicit waypoint or goal executor: the predicted future supplies targets for separate execution stage, rather than only features inside an action head. In Demo-JEPAs real-robot comparison, the diffusion action head has higher mean success on familiar behavior grounding, while planning has higher mean success on unseen tasks. The familiar-task advantage does not persist in its simulation comparison. The relative value of search and learned decoding depends on both task novelty and the execution setting, even when the two share future representation. Prediction can also supply route or discrete transition model. TADreamer reconstructs navigation waypoints from generated video and registers them to measured geometry before planning [335]; metric calibration connects imagined motion to feasible execution. GAVEL instead rolls plans through an explicit graph of action preconditions, effects, and location beliefs, repairing model-detectable violations before invoking semantic replanning [336]. Their shared predictive interface does not require common visual representation. Human-video world-action systems broaden the intermediate toward robot-domain visual evolution. Two dependencies become central: current robot progress must determine which part of the demonstration remains relevant [23], and the demonstrated procedure must change the predicted future even when the current scene admits familiar continuation [24]. These dependencies connect the older goal-reaching formulation to one-shot task transfer. The predicted evolution must preserve the procedure selected by the example. The two dependencies operate over different timescales. demonstration supplies procedure that should persist, whereas recent robot observations determine the next physically relevant transition. WorldScape Policy 2.0 combines persistent demonstration context, event-level memory, and short-term visual dynamics within joint videoaction model [25]. This moves the design problem beyond choosing RGB or latent futures: the model must keep the taught procedure stable while updating its account of the scene. Memory preserves the procedure while prediction tracks its current physical realization. The planning and control clocks can be separated explicitly. MaP-WAM uses sparse observed segment histories to generate language subgoal and visual plan; its executor reuses the cached plan until progress In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications Figure 11 Two roles of visual prediction: training (left) and deployment (right). Flames mark trainable modules; snowflakes mark fixed modules. (a) SynthICL trains the context layers and both heads, then removes the subgoal head; its frozen DINOv3 backbone is omitted [77]. (b) Zero-WAM trains the video and action branches, then freezes both and replaces recorded future video with generated video [24]. estimates trigger another planning step [401]. Matching the current observation to nearby plan frames calibrates that progress. At transition, actual execution frames replace the imagined plan in episodic memory. This separation matters: forecast can guide action, but recording it as an achieved event would let prediction errors become historical evidence. The executors auxiliary future-video head can be omitted at inference, while the upstream visual plan remains part of deployed control. Retrieval can constrain prediction before detailed motion is generated. The retrieval-augmented policy ReCAP supplies trajectories to frozen residual predictor [152]; its Cosmos Policy branch jointly generates future images and actions. The retrieved motion narrows the continuation, while prediction relates it to the evolving scene. Other ReCAP backbones route retrieved evidence through different action interfaces, so the predictive classification applies to its Cosmos Policy branch. The gain in inspectability comes with new failure mode. predicted scene can express the correct intention yet be unreachable, miss necessary contact, or accumulate error during execution. Pixel prediction retains appearance detail at computational cost; latent prediction offers compression but makes the retained task detail less visible. Action-conditioned simulation, goal-conditioned generation, and joint actionworld policies consequently use related representations for different purposes [180]. The value of the intermediate depends on how reliably its task information survives conversion into executable motion. Learning from futures without executing through them. Future supervision can improve an action representation without requiring future to be generated online. Let La be an action-training loss and Lv an auxiliary future-prediction loss. The training and deployment interfaces can then be written as θ arg min θ (cid:2)La(θ) + λLv(θ)(cid:3), At πθ ( ht, Ct). (12) Here λ 0 weights the auxiliary loss. Optimization acts on the designated trainable components, with any frozen backbone held fixed. The retained components of θ initialize the deployed parameters θ0; the auxiliary prediction head can be removed when action generation does not depend on its output. Equation (10), by comparison, retains future-dependent action computation at deployment. geometric intermediate can improve training without becoming an online execution dependency. Gripper traces provide motion-specific supervision, while reasoning dropout or removal of the future-trace head 25 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications permits execution without generating those traces [181, 182]. The learned action representation then carries the benefit, avoiding separate prediction stage at each decision. Internal semantic reasoning can play similar role: PonderPounce conditions action inference on an asynchronous cognition token while keeping subgoal text inside the model [183]. The intermediate shapes the representation used for action inference. The distinction is therefore between two computational roles of prediction (Figure 11). In auxiliary predictive supervision, future targets shape the policy during training, but actions do not depend on an explicit future prediction at deployment. In prediction-conditioned control, the predicted future remains an input to action generation. In panel (a), context layers denote the trainable context and statecontext transformers after the frozen visual backbone. In panel (b), the video and action blocks denote the trainable prediction branches, not the input frames. Auxiliary prediction strengthens the representation used by context-conditioned policy. Deployment-time predictions guide execution directly, coupling control quality to the generated future. Predictive control separates task interpretation from its physical realization through an anticipated consequence. The anticipated consequence exposes an intermediate for inspection or planning. Its contribution to control depends on both forecast accuracy and the action interface that realizes it, making prediction and decoding distinct sources of error. Skilland agent-based execution makes different abstraction: it specifies operations and delegates their consequences to available skills or tools.

sections.title: 3.4 Skill- and agent-based execution
sections.content: Skilland agent-based execution assumes that existing skills or robot tools can realize task once context has specified their selection, order, and arguments. video showing red block placed in the left bin before blue block enters the right bin can become an ordered procedure. The executor supplies the available motor competence; contextual inference determines how to use it. Two branches make this separation concrete: learned skill composition and VLM and LLM agents that generate programs or tool requests. After defining their common specificationexecutor interface, we compare these branches and use feedback-driven revision to show when changed specification suffices and when execution itself must be learned. The specification can take the form of code, spatial targets, or an ordered sequence of learned skills. Its defining role is to govern an execution stage that can track or advance it, as described in Section 2. At that action interface, the deterministic form is = fθ(Ct, ht), At = κ(g, ot), (13) where fθ extracts the execution specification from context Ct and robot history ht, and κ realizes it as the next action block At using observation ot. For stochastic specification generation and execution, the same interface becomes πθ(At ht, Ct) = kθ(At g, ht) pg θ(g Ct, ht) dg. (14) Here pg θ generates execution specifications and kθ is the executors action distribution. Discrete programs or skills replace the integral with sum; deterministic generation and execution recover Equation (13). In this family, specifies operations, their arguments, or their composition for separate executor. transferred geometric reference belongs to the geometric family when reference tracking is the primary dependency; hybrids can combine both interfaces. predicted future can also be decoded into g, composing this interface with world-model-based control. Neural components of the executor belong to θ; numerical arguments and generated code belong to g. Revising these arguments or code can change behavior without training the executors neural weights.

sections.title: Skill composition and program execution instantiate this interface as
sections.content: Skill composition: Program synthesis: = (z1, . . . , zNg ), At = κ(zℓt, ot), = fθ(Ct, ht), At = Run(g, ht). (15) In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications In the first row, ℓ indexes skills, zℓ is skill specification, Ng is the number of skills, and ℓt {1, . . . , Ng} identifies the active skill. In the second, fθ generates program g, and Run executes it until it produces the next action block, including permitted perception and control calls. Tool-using agents can generate one request at time: the tool name and arguments form g, the robot adapter implements κ, and its returned observation updates the next decision. generated program may call geometric tracker, thereby composing this family with geometric demonstration transfer. Composing reusable skills. An early insight was that rearranging existing motor capabilities can express new task. Neural Task Programming [26] made this explicit in 2017: demonstration instantiated hierarchy whose leaves invoked robot routines. The transferable knowledge was the decomposition and its arguments, while execution reused the available primitives. This separated generalization in task length, ordering, and object assignments from learning the physical skills themselves. Human-video teaching requires recognizing behavior across bodies, scenes, and timing. XSkill learns shared humanrobot skill prototypes [29]; UniSkill scales skill representation learning to unaligned cross-embodiment video [30]. Both use human examples to guide robot-side skill-conditioned policy, extending the interface from reordering known routines to recognizing transferable behavior in another bodys demonstration. Skill abstraction must preserve the taught distinction: attributed waypoints retain motion targets [164], object-relation graphs retain dependencies [165], and interaction-aware procedures retain stage changes [93]. The executors interface determines which of these constraints reaches motion. Semantic subtasks can alternatively condition continuous action predictor internally, as in StellaVLA [163]. An abstractions computational role therefore depends on whether it supplies separate executor or the policys own action inference. composed procedure also needs evidence for when to advance. StageGuard distills demonstration-grounded completion reasoning into lightweight monitor that decides whether to continue, advance, or skip skill [337]. Navi-Agent verifies local navigation subgoals against persistent topology of visual places and executed transitions [338]. Observed progress governs advancement through the composed procedure. Navigation illustrates two levels of example-conditioned execution. Instructionlandmark examples in LMNav [359] and instructionsubtask examples in A2Nav [360] guide language parser that specifies what pretrained navigators should execute. Select2Plan [352] retrieves visual decision examples for selecting marked movements or waypoints. The reasoning output is an executable choice, while motion realization belongs to the available navigator. Terrain feedback can further change the costs attached to those choices, as in VLM-GroNav [353]. Section 6.2 compares the information supplied by these contexts. VLM and LLM agents: programs, tools, and feedback. Language-model pretraining expanded adaptation to program generation in 2022. Code as Policies [27] uses commandprogram examples to recombine perception, control, arithmetic, and feedback logic; program examples also specify available objects and interfaces [28]. Multimodal reasoning extends this route to demonstrated procedures. Show-Harness converts video frames into textual outline for an unchanged planner and an embodiment-specific action interpreter [31]. The outline carries procedural structure into execution; spatial and contact constraints must also appear in this representation to guide the action interpreter. Preserving contact structure requires richer executable abstraction. RAPID derives local trajectoryoptimization primitives, relational composition constraints, and reconstructed verification environment from human demonstration [390]. The inferred predicates and simulated scene variants support iterative program revision before the resulting primitives and strategy are frozen for transfer. Compared with an outline over supplied skills, teaching here helps construct both the available operations and their checks. Transfer depends on whether the inferred relations preserve the demonstrated interaction and whether reconstruction makes verification physically informative. Its nonprehensile experiments support this demonstration-conditioned pathway; the separate LIBERO-Pro experiment instead constructs programs without demonstrations. Reconstruction and program search contribute to the time and interaction needed to acquire the new task. The command interface determines which decisions contextual inference must resolve. GPT-Policy uses goal images or demonstrations, available state and action records, and interaction feedback to request Cartesian 27 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications targets or gripper commands [94]. RoboDawn instead grounds discrete translation, rotation, and gripper commands through in-context examples [365]. In both cases, fixed models request actions from existing motor competence and use returned feedback to revise subsequent requests. Tools expand the evidence and behavior available to this inference. Robo-Harness K1 exposes calibrated depth, spatial measurements, persistent visual anchors, and grasp hypotheses to ground generic motion requests [379]. The agentic framework RACaP exposes typed Policy APIs: ReAct agent combines working memory, retrieved experience, and visual feedback to choose calls, arguments, and recovery steps [380]. Both retain fixed neural weights during deployment; RACaP also freezes its generated source code. The memoryexecutor interface sets another limit. In 2AM, the agent retains task history but sends only subtask language and optional 2D grasp, place, and move hints to an episodically stateless action model [403]. These cues bind remembered intent to current-image instances without asking the agent to produce robot trajectories. Their validity differs: grasp cue expires after acquisition, whereas destination can persist during transport. The action model is trained to interpret noisy or incomplete hints. External task memory works through learned steering interface. Its expressiveness determines which temporal and contact-dependent requirements can reach the action model. Previewable actions add further use of context: candidate can be revised before it changes the scene. World Action Agent (WAA) selects interaction-centered views, renders proposed poses with kinematic planning feedback, and converts in-view corrections into robot motion [388]. Its main agent consults separate Skill Agent for demonstration-derived procedures and visual checks. Tool requests form the execution specification, while geometric planning checks their feasibility before control. After execution, the interface determines which feedback reaches the next decision. ETA, implemented in OpenETA [349], requires fresh observation after each world-changing tool call. RoboHarness addresses transitions between pretrained policies with different operating conditions: execution memory selects policy and retrieves states that guide entry into its operating region [350]. Feedback thus supports both revising an action and selecting the competence needed to execute it. Generated programs can also construct spatial affordance and constraint maps for geometric motion planning [184]. The interface allocates competence: named pick-and-place routine supplies perception and grasp synthesis, whereas pose-level control exposes those decisions to the agent. Improved success may consequently reflect stronger supplied executor as well as better contextual inference. plausible procedure can still request an action that the current scene cannot support. Skill-affordance estimates address this gap before execution by coupling linguistic relevance to physical feasibility [185]. Scene and execution feedback address it after transition by revising what should happen next [186]. When feasibility depends on an unknown property, targeted measurements such as proprioceptive estimates of mass or stiffness can change the manipulation strategy [187]. These are complementary uses of evidence: predict applicability, observe the outcome, and acquire information missing from either. They connect program-level reasoning to the actual conditions under which skill works. Feedback-driven revision changes either the procedure or the learned capability used to execute it. frozen language model can adjust primitives direction, distance, or duration from outcome errors [9]; these values remain arguments of g. CaP-X contrasts feedback-driven code generation with reinforcement learning of the coding policy [166]. ENPIRE exposes both choices within physical experimentation: revise perception and control programs, or collect experience to train neural policy [89]. VoxPosers online dynamics-learning extension similarly changes learned component [184]. The practical distinction is what the correction must supply. Recombining available operations changes their use; acquiring missing predictive or motor capability requires learning process for that component. Across these forms, explicit structure exposes task order, constraints, and intervention points. Its central trade-off is portability versus physical detail: compact procedure can cross scenes and bodies while omitting required grasp or compliance condition. The executor can recompute only details left open by the teaching. DualManip separates the corresponding update rates: live geometric correspondence revises grasp contacts 28 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications Figure 12 Four technical paradigms convert context into actions through (a) direct action inference, (b) geometric motion-reference transfer, (c) prediction-conditioned control, and (d) skill or tool execution. Representative implementations are Vid2Robot [14], SemAnCorr [38], Zero-WAM [24], and UniSkill [30], respectively. while semantic reasoning is invoked when geometric validation fails [410]. This hybrid preserves task intent across motion without requiring full replanning for every observation. Table 5 separates context operations from their carriers. Encode commonly supports learned future prediction or skill inference; Parse exposes procedures and calls; Retrieve and Verify can augment either route. video can become future, motion reference, skill, or program, each preserving different task constraints for its executor. The execution column exposes second difference: predicted future can guide planning or condition action decoding, while motion reference can support tracking or replay. The carrier and execution operation jointly specify the transfer assumption. Choosing an interface by the constraint it preserves. useful interface preserves the task distinction most likely to be lost before execution. Direct action inference can exploit learned correspondence when the teaching resembles its training relationships. Geometric transfer exposes binding contact or relative motion for inspection and tracking. Predictive control makes consequences available for selection, while skill and program interfaces expose ordering and preconditions. These choices relocate the generalization burden: to the learned interpreter, the matched interaction, the future model, or the supplied executor. Hybrids compose these assumptions. predicted future can yield waypoints, and program can invoke geometric tracker. Their placement follows the intermediate that carries the demonstrated requirement into execution, allowing hybrid to combine several families.

sections.title: 3.5 Shared mechanisms: correspondence and memory
sections.content: All four interfaces face three linked requirements. taught task must first be bound to the objects in the current scene, including replacements for those in the demonstration. Its evidence must remain available at the decision that needs it, and its interpretation must express change the controller can execute. The discussion therefore moves from transfer across objects to access across time and then to the command interface that realizes correction. Figure 12 shows the intermediates passed to control: attended demonstration features, transferred contact frames, predicted robot future, and skill sequence. Evidence selection and interpretation (Figure 10) precede these computations. What changes Held vessel Held vessel Receiver Both objects Jug bottle Same jug Jug bottle Receiver Same cup Cup bowl Cup bowl Motion adjustments Grasp; tilt angle Pouring position; height Grasp; tilt; pouring position Cross-object transfer of demonstrated tasks. demonstration can specify relation that remains meaningful after its objects are replaced. Consider robot shown how to pour from jug into cup. It may then use bottle with the same cup, keep the jug but pour into bowl, or use both the bottle and the bowl. Table 6 contrasts these three settings using this illustrative task. The held vessel is the manipulated object; the cup or bowl is the receiving object, role that can also be support or contact surface in other tasks. Each role can change within category or through functionally compatible substitute. Novelty relative to the demonstration and novelty relative to training remain separate properties. We first examine which relations transfer between new instances, then consider functional substitution and the control needed to realize the transferred requirement. 30 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications In this example, the robot must still direct the liquid into the receiver. bottle can require different grasp and tilt angle from the demonstrated jug; bowl can require different pouring position and height from the cup. Replacing both couples these adjustments: the new vessel must be grasped and oriented so that its outlet directs the flow into the new opening. The transferred requirement is thus preserved while the motion changes. Each setting isolates different set of coupled geometric adjustments. From object identity to task-relevant relations. An unchanged object in new pose often permits relocation of reference. new instance can change the grasp, contact surface, or clearance even when its role stays fixed. R-NDF transfers relations such as placing bowl on mug or bottle in container to previously unseen object pairs [346]. Its original setting uses five to ten demonstrations with pretrained category representations and marked 3D keypoint. Descriptor alignment recomputes placement with those representations fixed; the paper also studies learned energy-based refinement, which requires training an additional neural component. part-based representation supports one-demonstration transfer across larger shape variation [347]. Its real-robot tests include new mugrack and bowlmug pairs, using learned part models and segmentation assistance. These results connect the relation shown in demonstration to execution on new objects while exposing the prior geometry and human input that make the transfer possible. From new instances to functional substitutes. Category changes make the preserved role more important than whole-object similarity. FUNCTO transfers tool use from an actionless human RGB-D video and task description, distinguishing spatial, instance, and category generalization [172]. Its functional keypoints locate how replacement tool should be grasped and used; the experiments emphasize tool variation, with less emphasis on changes to the receiving object. SemAnCorr transfers pouring motion from kettle to toy cup and cutting motion from scissors to nail clipper, using recorded contact and motion from kinesthetic teaching [38]. These different evidence interfaces support functional correspondence without requiring common demonstration format. Cross-category matching can also be supplied: the part-decomposition study evaluates pre-pouring alignment for watering-can substitution using provided part equivalencies [347]. This protocol isolates geometric alignment with the cross-object correspondence already specified. Functional substitution must preserve the requirement actually taught. general request to transfer contents can admit another vessel; specified vessel or handle contact can remove that freedom. At higher level of abstraction, preserving purpose may require different procedure rather than transformed motion. The Imitator Game distinguishes category-preserving substitution from this affordance-adapted imitation [101]. The invariant is therefore task-dependent choice: object relation, contact constraint, process, or intended effect. Section 7.1 tests whether the demonstration determines that choice. Realizing transferred requirement. The four control interfaces consume this requirement differently. context-conditioned policy can bind it within action features; geometric transfer exposes reference; predictive control can express desired future; and skill or program can bind its arguments to new objects. Each interface preserves the requirement in different form for its executor. Geometry used to train policy [189, 190] also differs from reference supplied at deployment or demonstration-fitted motion system [191]. Likewise, spatial affordance prediction and spatial action representations provide useful priors [192, 193]; newly supplied demonstration must still determine which requirement the prior should realize. Relational skill guidance provides an agent-based route to transfer. WAAs frozen LIBERO-derived skills transfer to robosuite lifting, stacking, and restacking, where objects, scenes, and viewpoints change; grounding resolves poses from the current scene [388]. When interpretation produces desired pose or feature configuration, separate controller can track it. For stationary target, local visual-servo rule is et = st , qt = kvsJ vis,tet. (16) Here st and are current and desired visual features, et their error, qt the joint configuration, and Jvis,t the feature Jacobian. Its pseudoinverse and positive gain kvs map feature error to joint velocity [194]. Context changes the reference while feedback corrects its realization. New contact or dynamics can still invalidate that realization, even with correct correspondence. The final part of this subsection examines 31 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications this execution boundary. Transfer also requires the defining evidence to remain accessible when needed, motivating the memory mechanisms below. Accessing and updating evidence across time. Alignment selects information within demonstration, retrieval selects records from an archive, and memory preserves evidence across decisions. These operations can expose policy examples, motion references, predicted rollouts, or programs. The retrieved objects use in control determines its method family; the access mechanism itself does not. useful memory must answer three questions: which fact matters, how it can be recovered, and when it stops being valid. Task requirements, physical-response estimates, and completed-step records need different update rules  (Table 7)  . moved part can invalidate its remembered pose while leaving the taught order intact. The readupdate decomposition separates stored evidence from the policy input; subsequent comparisons relate selection, compression, and reset timing to the decision they support. Sections 5 and 8.4 develop validity during execution and reuse. Carrying evidence between decisions. recurrent state mt and an external archive Mt provide complementary ways of retaining experience. Let xt = (ot, at, ot+1) be an executed transition, augmented with feedback when available. common readupdate decomposition is mt+1 = uθ(mt, xt), Mt+1 = wθ(Mt, xt), Rt = ρθ(ht, Mt), Ct = bθ(C task , mt, Rt). (17) The maps uθ and wθ update recurrent and external memory, ρθ retrieves records Rt, and bθ constructs the policy input. The supplied task evidence task includes instructions, goals, examples, and newly received corrections in any supported modality; it reduces to Ds in demonstration-only configuration. The retained state (mt, Mt) and the selected input Ct are distinct. An implementation may omit either memory component, and its maps may combine analytic operations with fixed neural components. This decomposition generalizes the self-contained update in Equation (2) without restricting context to demonstrations. Retaining the information that changes control. Early latent task inference compressed transitions to identify reward or dynamics [196, 197]. Selective retention matters because demonstrators collection style can correlate with task identity in training logs without identifying the task reliably at deployment. Physical adaptation depends on when evidence is acquired and how long it remains relevant. RMA uses recent task transitions; ICWM collects task-agnostic probes; LocoFormer carries interaction across trials [3941]. RopeFormer extends cross-trial actionresponse conditioning to dynamic ropes, retaining policy context while resetting the physical trial [364]. Zeva and Zeva-Ego instead encode action effects at two timescales; the latter combines recent within-attempt traces with phase-matched memory across attempts on the same task instance [88, 363]. These fixed-weight interfaces trade the cost of collecting evidence against its relevance to subsequent control. Event memory addresses different representation need: an earlier observation may establish that button was pressed, even when the current scene no longer reveals that event. Perceptual retrieval and semantic event records preserve such evidence with different detail and processing costs [4244]. Recurrent designs compress visual history at frame or action-chunk timescales [198, 199]; event-triggered storage retains selected raw keyframes [200]. MemBodied combines fixed-size associative interaction state with an initial-scene anchor, preserving early evidence alongside later updates [381]. ARMS addresses concurrent execution by asynchronously supplying perception, embodied state, and records of which arm acted and when [387]. These designs retain different temporal structure: stable reference, accumulated events, or actor-specific action history. Their deployed memory updates change the evidence read by trained policy. HIRE retains ordered wrench traces to distinguish visually aliased interaction states, coupling this history-conditioned action inference to faster contact executor [404]. Its shuffled-history comparison tests whether temporal order, rather than force availability alone, supplies the missing state evidence. Explicit memory can expose the binding that compressed state leaves implicit. Mimir separates world facts from task progress, retrieving candidates for the active goal and marking completion only when feedback supports its postcondition [394]. OCC4M makes complementary distinction between persistent object 32 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications identity and remembered place [395]. selected objects target follows its updated track; historicallocation target remains fixed and is reprojected into the current view. Together, these designs show why memory must preserve the intended referent and its update rule. Object motion updates tracked referent, while task progress advances after the required postcondition is observed. OCC4M evaluates moving views in simulation with calibrated support geometry and uses fixed camera in its hardware study. Past evidence and imagined futures answer different temporal questions. An observation window establishes what happened, as in SimpleMemVLA [45]; combining retrieved events with imagined states, as in MemoryVLA++, adds what could happen next [209]. Acquiring new rule for what to remember poses further generalization problem. In µVLA, recurrence helps held-out tasks with familiar memory requirements but yields little improvement when the required memory structure changes [199]. The distinction is between recalling evidence under learned rule and inferring which evidence an unfamiliar task makes relevant. Where selection is performed changes both cost and flexibility. Workspace Models move VLM-based saliency selection into training: an encoder learns latent workspace tokens by reconstructing selected historical image patches, and downstream policy learns to act from those tokens [397]. This amortizes online reasoning but also inherits the saliency supervisions information choices. comparison with runtime retrieval can vary decision latency and memory demand together, testing both familiar event recall and the retention of new teaching. History can also reconstruct an unobserved part of the present, rather than past event or future consequence. LIFD combines recurrent evidence with geometry-anchored scene-token completion before action prediction [339]. This distinction matters for classification: generating missing current state supports context-conditioned inference, whereas world-model-based control requires predicted consequences on the execution path. Selecting, compressing, and using history. The benefit of memory depends on which event survives compression and whether the current decision needs it. Selection and ordering already matter in language ICL [124]; robotics adds short physical events whose removal changes the meaning of an otherwise similar trajectory. Robust Instant Policys downsampling study identifies the loss of brief events such as grasp transition [201]; its full system additionally fits policy at deployment. The useful horizon follows the unknown. AMAGOs MetaWorld ML-1 analysis finds that short histories can identify hidden goals, while longer contexts can reduce sample efficiency [202]. ReLIC instead reuses experience across episodes to locate objects in an unfamiliar home, with deployed neural parameters fixed [203]. Section 6.2 relates this longer horizon to acquisition of spatial knowledge. Retrieval faces two decisions: which event answers the current uncertainty, and whether that uncertainty requires history at all. Question-answering supervision can teach relevance, as in HALO [204]; calibrated history gate can give current observations precedence when they already suffice [105]. The decisions expose different errors: missing relevant event or allowing an irrelevant record to override the current scene. For an archive Mt = {ξj}Nt be candidate set of record indices and Jt the selected set. budgeted retrieval rule is j=1, ξj is its jth record and Nt is the number of records available at decision t. Let Jt arg max J{1,...,Nt}, JK jJ (cid:2)sθ(ht, ξj) η(cid:3), Rt = (ξj)jJt. (18) Here counts selected records, is the maximum record count, and η is the relevance threshold. The compatibility score sθ is used as in Equation (6), with an archive record as its second argument. The retrieved sequence Rt contains the records indexed by Jt. fixed ordering rule arranges selected records in Rt; fixed tie rule resolves equal scores. The empty set permits read with no useful history. sections.title: 3.6 External knowledge reuse and revision
sections.content: External knowledge reuse retains lesson or executable artifact beyond the attempt that produced it. Three forms have different consequences: guidance changes later inference, callable routines enlarge the available repertoire, and revised context or verification code changes how the system uses evidence. Table B3 in Appendix records these update objects. The analysis first separates acquisition from reuse, then compares the three forms before considering consolidation into neural parameters. This progression connects immediate contextual adaptation to reuse and then to improvements in subsequent learning. To separate within-attempt inference from persistent adaptation, let Bn collect the external artifacts retained before attempt n: memory records, skill code, controller code and its numerical settings, or contextconstruction code. Let Tn be the executed trace and feedback from that attempt. proposal-and-validation loop has the form eBn+1 Fθ( Bn, Tn), Bn+1 = ( eBn+1, χn = 1, χn = 0, Bn, θ = θ0. (19) The fixed model Fθ generates proposed artifact collection eBn+1; the tilde marks candidate awaiting validation. The acceptance indicator χn {0, 1} is one for acceptance and zero for rejection under the systems validation procedure, potentially including additional rollouts. Writing the effective policy as πθ(At ht, Ct; Bn) makes this external dependence explicit. The next attempt uses Bn+1 to construct context or execute commands. In skilland agent-based execution, accepted artifacts can select an executor κBn or determine the program and its numerical arguments. These generated code and settings belong to the external artifacts; learned 35 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications neural parameters of any executor remain part of θ. Systems without separate acceptance gate use χn = 1. The attempt index differs from the decision index t: one artifact revision can involve several model calls and robot transitions. Section 7.2 accounts for the trials needed to acquire and validate the artifact before measuring reuse. Table 8 groups external artifacts by their role in execution; Table B3 (p. 98) further separates plans from executable programs. procedural plan specifies an explicit step sequence or outline. Reusable guidance stores acquired rules, applicability conditions, or annotated lessons. An executable repertoire contains separately addressable skills, routines, or motion primitives; program or its settings specifies the task controller. Execution oversight uses code that constructs model inputs or implements separate verifier, monitor, or intervention mechanism. Checks embedded in the task program belong to that program. These objects can coexist: stored lesson guides subsequent synthesis, while callable function directly extends the execution vocabulary. Two uses of the retained artifacts explain how this update reaches control: Guidance reuse: Ct = bθ(C task Executable reuse: = fθ(Ct, ht; Bn), , mt, Rt; Bn), At πθ( ht, Ct), At = κBn (g, ot). (20) The context builder bθ and memory inputs are those of Equation (17); the semicolon makes dependence on the retained artifacts Bn explicit. Guidance reuse changes the evidence supplied to otherwise unchanged control. Executable reuse makes the retained library or controller implementation available to specification generation and execution; κBn denotes that artifact-dependent executor. Both may occur in one system. Together, Equations (19) and (20) connect an artifacts acquisition to its later use under fixed neural parameters θ. Grounding an interface and learning through it. Show-Harness makes the distinction concrete. Its VLM selects semantic motion commands, while body-specific interpreter supplies calibrated execution. Video can specify an otherwise missing task order. Yet the action-representation experiment shows that reading explicit command conventions is substantially easier than discovering arbitrary command meanings through probing [31]. The former supplies correspondence; the latter requires inferring it from action effects. The interpreter supplies the low-level control in both conditions. High-level commands leave grasp synthesis and feedback control to the executor; lower-level commands require the model to resolve more geometry and timing. Guava compares this allocation through workflows and action abstractions [211], while compositions of frozen motor capabilities, planning, and verification expose its system-level effect [212]. This allocation determines how existing competence is used; context interventions identify the additional task information supplied by examples or interaction. SkipVLA makes this allocation explicit within hybrid policy: classical planner handles free-space transit, while the instruction-conditioned VLA handles contact-rich motion [340]. Its learned target predictor connects the two. The routing design improves execution efficiency by assigning transit and contact to interfaces suited to their respective demands. The first extension is from open-loop synthesis to outcome-conditioned revision. Textual feedback can revise plan [186]; intermediate observations can revise the plan and Python controller separately [213]; program checks can make some responses executable without another model call [28]. Constraint violations narrow revisions to code and sampling bounds [214], while primitive-level errors narrow them to control settings [9]. These interfaces determine the available edit space. Section 5 addresses the separate question of which edit the observed failure justifies. Retaining guidance and executable routines. Reuse asks which part of successful repair remains valid later. Constraints attached to plan or code revisions preserve its scope [46]; causal annotations explain its effect [215]; distilled rules and code patterns support later synthesis [48]. Attribution determines the appropriate change: failure to follow valid guidance calls for execution repair, while defective skill may require revising guidance or code [216]. Retaining the cause helps avoid inappropriate reuse. 36 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications Visual evidence makes retained guidance more explicit. WAA turns expert demonstrations and human corrections into procedures with applicability conditions, reference images, and outcome checks [388]. In its one-demonstration stove study, review replaces knob motion as the success criterion with an observed activation signal. Fixed agents then interpret the acquired guidance. Executable reuse makes recurring behavior callable. Function synthesis supplies missing operations [27]; program clustering and human feedback refine reusable candidates [50, 51]. Video-grounded retrieval supplies implementation details such as contacts and target poses [217], while repeated successful code can enter library [166]. Transfer then depends on scene-specific arguments and valid execution preconditions. Autonomous trials can supply the evidence previously provided by teachers correction, but the retained object determines what later tasks gain. Rewriting controller improves the current solution [218]; taskagnostic play can accumulate code skills and failure records for later use [52]. Distilling validated repair into failure signature, applicability condition, and strategy instead retains guidance for constructing future solution [47]. These routes share outcome-driven acquisition while transferring different knowledge: specific implementation, callable operation, or rule for choosing repair. structured library also supports failure attribution. RoboRSI organizes diagnosis and revision through taskskill tree, retaining successful workflows as callable code [348]. Its code-on/code-off comparison reports 174/600 versus 129/600 successes over 120 tasks and five layouts each. This tests retained routines; its separate policy-training case consolidates corrective trajectories into neural parameters. The retained object distinguishes these two forms of reuse. Separating semantic effects from geometric realization supports reuse across scenes. Teach and Grows Skill Blocks specify effects, scope, executors, verification, and recovery [53]. Its simulation pilot evaluates local library additions with deterministic decomposition and fixed executor; agent-based induction and Experience Memory updates remain proposed. The evaluated contribution expands repertoire, while the proposed extension would learn how to build it. Reuse can encompass complete closed-loop policy. Programs refined through demonstrations and simulation feedback become examples for new policy generation [341]. Generalized TAMP experiments similarly separate simulator-assisted code synthesis from evaluation of frozen programs on unseen instances [407]. RIVET makes the interface explicit: generated perception and planning programs share object poses and relation graph, then operate without runtime VLM regeneration [408]. HuGo instead refines high-level policy code from rollout trajectories and video while preserving frozen whole-body controller [409]. Together, these designs locate adaptation in program construction and revision; subsequent execution tests whether the acquired logic transfers beyond its synthesis trials. Adapting how evidence reaches control. Retained guidance improves how available routines are invoked. Parameterized call sequences preserve useful orderings, while global heuristics describe the operating conditions and failures of fixed primitives [207]. Hi-VLAs tabletop study likewise finds greater benefits from prior-episode affordance summaries than longer within-episode history [219]. Such memory captures conditions of use, connecting agent reasoning to system identification of available capabilities. Repeated failures in evidence selection or verification motivate adapting the surrounding inference procedure. Revising history-selection code changes what the planner can see; revising critic or recovery tool changes how execution is checked and corrected. SHAPER targets procedural guidance and context construction with the planner and executor fixed [49]; Zetta targets critics, recovery tools, and governance around frozen policy [90]. RACaP jointly evolves Policy APIs, the ReAct harness, and experience memory before freezing the resulting system for deployment [380]. This separates two timescales: external-artifact revision improves the available interface, whereas runtime context selects how the current task uses it. Compiling repair also changes when reasoning is paid for. HarnessPAI retains task program during each rollout, including observation-conditioned checks, and revises it between rollouts using stage-indexed failure-to-repair memory [398]. Its program-level open loop therefore still permits sensor feedback during execution. This amortizes synthesis across repeated tasks, while changed instruction or operating condition can require renewed validation. Its skill-library comparison shows faster program convergence on three 37 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications representative development tasks. Held-out acquisition tests would measure how this benefit transfers to subsequent learning. In its LIBERO evaluations, the reported 50 seeds include 15 used for program evolution, distinction relevant to interpreting transfer. Connecting contextual acquisition to neural consolidation. Neural consolidation turns acquired experience into future model competence. Distilling harness interaction traces [211, 388] or combining orchestration with autonomous data collection and policy refinement [220] transfers work initially performed through inference into trained parameters. EmbodiedSWE diversifies verified agent solutions into demonstrations for VLA training [382], supplying variations beyond the solved task instances. The training target determines what is consolidated: successful trajectories teach execution, whereas successful teaching exchanges, as in LMPC, teach responsiveness to later feedback [117]. Section 8.5 develops this distinction. The next chapter examines how training data connect task evidence to execution. Takeaways ① Context determines an action distribution, geometric reference, predicted consequences, or an execution specification. Equations (4), (7), (9), and (13) identify these four interfaces. ② Context interpretation and motor competence limit transfer separately. Retrieval and memory support transfer by supplying usable evidence to controller that responds to later corrections. ③ With neural weights fixed, context can revise task outlines, executable routines, and programs. Retaining these artifacts supports reuse, and successor comparisons measure their contribution to learning subsequent tasks.

sections.title: 4 Data and Training: How Is Context Use Learned?
sections.content: An input channel makes context accessible; training determines whether the policy uses it. When the current scene already identifies every target action, model can fit demonstrations without learning to consult earlier teaching. The central data question is therefore which relationships make earlier evidence informative about later decision. Acquisition sources determine what is measured, training units establish these relationships, and construction at scale supplies their missing variations. This connects the transfer assumptions of Section 3 to the experience needed to support them. Source taxonomies, such as the Data Pyramid survey [221], describe where embodied data originate and how closely they match robot execution. ICL for robots additionally asks what earlier teaching or interaction reveals about later decision. record's source, channels, and role in learning are therefore separate dimensions. Explicit pairs, continuous streams, and linked attempts organize these dimensions differently; pretrained interpretation and geometric construction can also connect evidence to execution without jointly training the entire path.

sections.title: 4.1 Input sources and context modalities
sections.content: An acquisition source determines what is measured directly and what must be inferred. Teleoperation records robot commands, UMI estimates motion through robot-like device, egocentric video records human activity, and simulation provides modeled transitions. The four sources are compared on this common basis. Language can accompany every acquisition source. Instructions specify constraints, commandprogram examples establish conventions, corrections revise decisions, and summaries retain earlier events. Code as Policies, DROC, and MEM illustrate the latter three roles [27, 44, 46]. Records should preserve each statements source, time, and referent: teachers requested change and models interpretation of an event carry different evidence. Figure 13 contrasts the directly observed interaction: robot execution in teleoperation, instrumented hand motion in UMI, human activity in egocentric video, and modeled execution in simulation. These sources leave different correspondence problems for the learner, as the following parallel comparisons explain. Teleoperation: measurements and commanded interventions. real robot provides synchronized scene observations, measured robot state, and issued commands. DROID and BridgeData V2 supply such robot demonstrations [56, 58]; RH20T additionally records forcetorque measurements and, in one hardware 38 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications Figure 13 Four sources of contextual evidence for robots: (a) teleoperation, (b) UMI, (c) egocentric video, and (d) simulation. Their recordings differ in visual, state, action, and contact channels; language can accompany each as instructions, examples, or feedback. This control over the generating process is useful for contextual learning because procedure can be held fixed while scene geometry changes, or varied while the scene remains comparable. sections.title: 4.2 Training units and context dependence
sections.content: Channels become useful training evidence through temporal and task relationships. Table 11 compares paired episodes, continuous streams, and linked attempts. We define the temporal units first, then use supportquery supervision to distinguish input channels, action targets, and pairing criteria. Continuous experience and corrective records extend this dependency beyond explicit pairs. 40 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications Figure 14 Demonstrations serve three roles: (a) supervise motor actions, (b) train context use through paired episodes, and (c) specify new task to fixed policy. Panel (c) illustrates can-uprighting demonstration specifying stapler reorientation; it is conceptual example of cross-object transfer. Temporal units of contextual evidence. contextual training unit must identify what was observed, what was commanded, and what the resulting feedback established. Language can specify the intended task or annotate the outcome. The sequence must preserve when each item became available, so that later consequence can supervise learning without appearing as evidence for an earlier decision. Temporal alignment preserves the relation between an intervention and its consequence through sensor timestamps, command application times, coordinate conventions, and episode boundaries. Measured motor state must remain distinguishable from its command or setpoint. Aligned windows or timestamp-aware encoding accommodate different sampling rates while retaining brief contact events. Support can specify behavior or reveal an environment; query history locates execution; transitions reveal action consequences. These units overlap: history contains transitions, and retrieved segments can come from demonstrations or earlier attempts. Their role is independent of modality. Uprighting differently shaped object illustrates the third role: the operation must survive changed appearance. Paired supervision learns this dependency explicitly; continuous streams can expose it through the sequence of experience. Support channels and action supervision. Equation (21) supervises query actions while leaving support channels open. Vid2Robot conditions on video without recorded support commands [14]; ICRT supplies support actions in sensorimotor prefix [13]. Both supervise the query execution. Support content, the action loss, and the architecture that combines evidence are therefore separate choices. Task identity and supportquery pairing. The shared specification ψ determines the granularity of teaching. Pairing all executions labeled put the object away can preserve destination while discarding grasp or route preferences. BPP makes this dependence explicit in its task-grouped demonstrations [54]. The pairing rule must retain the distinction the deployment example is expected to convey. For cross-object transfer (Section 3.5), support and query can change the manipulated object, the receiver, or both while preserving the same requirement. Conversely, retaining comparable objects while varying the required relation makes the support informative. Together, these pairings separate task meaning from object identity and provide examples of which substitutions preserve the intended function. Pairing requires both semantic agreement and compatible action meaning. Additional demonstrations can distinguish task interpretations left ambiguous by one example, as Instant Policy illustrates with differently shaped boxes [16]. The resulting query target must still express the same intervention in consistent coordinates, timing, and gripper semantics. WALL-OSS-0.5 addresses this physical side through synchronized video and actions, camera repair, and end-effector calibration [233]. These requirements are complementary: semantic pairing determines which behavior is intended, while calibration determines what command realizes it. With shared action coordinates, each body retains its own reachability and contact mechanics. shared environment supplies different pairing relation from shared procedure. Route-following training pairs demonstrated path with perturbed execution, as in RPF [356]. Scene-conditioned training instead pairs preview with navigation to goals within that environment, as in NOLO [351]; ReLIC [203] links episodes in one home while changing the target and start. The shared variable is therefore the route in the first case and the environment in the latter two. Scene identity and memory-reset boundaries determine which spatial knowledge remains available across examples or episodes. From paired episodes to continuous experience. Explicit pairing makes the teachingexecution relationship part of the training unit. S1 supplies an in-context demonstration in its pretraining episodes [99]. GEN-1.5 instead reports next-action pretraining on randomly sampled continuous physical spans, without dedicated demonstration packing or an ICL-specific objective, and inserts sensorimotor examples as prompts at deployment [98]. stream exposes earlier observations and actions without assigning them separate support and query roles. Both systems later accept task examples, acquired through different organizations of training experience. Action generation is further choice: ContextFlow uses explicit robot supportquery supervision with continuous flow matching [55]. The action loss and the organization of experience play different roles: one fits the action model, while the other links preceding evidence to subsequent behavior. Behavioral diversity and contextual identifiability. Access to earlier evidence becomes useful when it resolves uncertainty about the continuation. If the current scene already determines every training action, the loss can be minimized without reading demonstration. Comparable scenes with different valid procedures instead give teaching predictive value; repetitions of one procedure across scenes teach which 42 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications Figure 15 Task diversity and prompting affect transfer differently. (a) BPP drawing error with 10,000 demonstrations, averaged over three seeds [54]. (b,c) S1 compares demonstration and language prompting on seen and unseen tasks; its cumulative per-step success measure includes human recovery interventions [99]. variations leave it unchanged. The practical consequence is to count distinguishable teaching problems as well as trajectories. The comparisons below examine this dependency, while Section 8.1 asks how far the resulting inference transfers. Context can also support shortcuts. Correlations with previous actions can improve imitation fit while impairing deployed control [234]; prefix may identify collection habits rather than task requirements. Varying demonstrators, procedures, and physical conditions independently helps separate these explanations. Holding out task relations, alongside trajectories, tests transfer beyond familiar procedures. Multiple valid procedures in comparable scenes support both contextual training and tests in which the supplied example changes the correct action (Section 7). The evidence distinguishes behavioral diversity from visual variety. ICRTs selected DROID-only training condition fails its test tasks, whereas its multi-task scenes require different actions from similar initial observations [13]. BPP supplies controlled allocation comparison: with 10,000 drawing demonstrations, mean Chamfer error is 9.5 pixels for 500 tasks with 20 demonstrations each, 5.1 for 1,000 tasks with ten each, and 3.4 for 2,000 tasks with five each (Figure 15a). Its less diverse folding setting can instead favor language conditioning [54]. Demo-JEPA separately varies task classes and trajectories per task [22]. Across these studies, useful diversity adds decisions that an example must resolve, supported by enough executions to learn the relationship. S1 separates scaling gains on seen and unseen tasks under matched data, compute, and architecture apart from the prompt embedding [99]. Across 1k100k training hours, both prompting methods improve on seen tasks. On unseen tasks, demonstration prompting rises from 1% to 66%, while language prompting rises from 0% to 9% (Figure 15b,c). Thus similar seen-task performance can conceal different returns to new-task teaching. The cumulative per-step metric includes human recovery, mainly for the language baseline. The S1 comparison concerns combined data scaling and prompting, while BPP directly isolates task diversity at fixed demonstration budget. Matching the procedural information conveyed by text and video would further isolate modality from teaching detail (Section 7.1). Linked attempts and corrective supervision. Learning from failed action or diagnostic probe extends context dependence across attempts. The training unit must link what was tried to what happened next, preserving reset boundaries and any change in the task or physical condition. Algorithm Distillation models such learning histories [6]; LocoFormer retains experience over varied morphologies and dynamics [40]. Reward-based meta-training can value an informative action through its benefit to later attempts [2]. short probe gains learning value when its outcome informs the next decision. Linked attempts expose this dependency during training. In recovery-conditioned supervision, the failed attempt and its feedback enter context while later continuation supplies corrective targets. RoboTTTs DAgger Distillation uses the full rollout as context but applies action loss only to human corrections, also improving its GDN comparator [10]. The failed actions 43 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications record what was tried; the selected corrections specify what to imitate. This training organization can support different memory mechanisms. Equation (21) extends to this case by replacing support-only conditioning with Ct. For block-level losses, includes only complete blocks composed entirely of actions selected for imitation. An objective supporting action-wise masking can instead suppress unselected positions within block. Other executed actions remain in history. The context mask controls available evidence, whereas the target mask controls desired behavior. Runtime context contains only evidence available before the decision; future outcomes may supply supervision. Attempt boundaries must separately record physical resets, memory resets, and changes of tool or dynamics. Long-context control requires representations that preserve decisive events. Past-Token Prediction adds reconstruction of earlier actions to future-action prediction, first learning short-context visual features and then caching them for longer-context training [235]. Caching reduces repeated computation; the cached visual features determine which task details remain available to the controller. The supervisory unit determines what evidence can explain later action: pairs link teaching to realization, streams link earlier events to current control, and linked attempts connect outcomes to revised decisions. Their common requirement is decision that earlier evidence helps disambiguate. The remaining analysis examines acquisition sources that preserve this dependency with usable action correspondence.

sections.title: 4.3 Data coverage and action correspondence
sections.content: Data coverage has two distinct meanings: the range of behavior recorded and the range of teachingexecution relationships recoverable from it. Robot records, motion-bearing human demonstrations, and ordinary video trade direct action correspondence against collection breadth. The comparison below follows that trade-off, asking which annotations make each source usable for contextual training. Simulation supplies controlled counterparts in Section 4.5; Table B4 lists resource-level details. From reusable experience to annotated procedures. Motor coverage supplies reusable behavior before teaching can specialize it. Autonomous multi-task experience and shared demonstration collections addressed this need [236, 237]; Bridge Data included 7,200 demonstrations across 71 tasks and ten environments. Later collections broadened scenes and embodiments [5658]. Contextual training additionally needs relationships between these executions that preserve what new example should teach. Procedure annotations identify why continuation changes. AgiBot Worlds March 2025 release spans 1,001,552 trajectories, 2,976.4 hours, 217 tasks, and 106 scenes, including subtask and recovery records [60]. Task intervals, step instructions, and later corrections connect demonstrations, autonomous attempts, and human interventions [238, 239]. Linking an attempt to its correction preserves the evidence that makes different continuation appropriate. Broader embodiment coverage makes shared task meaning and shared action meaning increasingly separate problems. Galaxeas common platform and subtask timing provide comparatively consistent collection interface [61]; RoboMIND 2.0 and RoboCOIN broaden the range of platforms [240242]. Procedural metadata identifies which executions teach the same requirement, while kinematic metadata describes how their realization differs. cross-body pair needs both. This explains why adding embodiments can expand motor coverage while increasing the work needed to construct reliable contextual pairs. Robot records supply executable supervision. Robot records become contextual supervision when query execution is associated with an example of its intended procedure [5658, 60]. Cross-scene retrieval can locate candidate executions [243], but matching must distinguish alternatives that begin in similar scenes. Humanrobot pairing exposes an asymmetry between teaching and supervision. human video can specify the intended interaction, while robot measurements reveal the commands and contact response needed to realize it. RH20T provides corresponding human videos together with robot images, joints, gripper state, forcetorque signals, audio, and tactile sensing in one configuration [59]. These richer query records can supervise policy whose eventual human support contains fewer channels. Task-level humanrobot organization helps define the transfer setting [101], but shared label such as fold can still merge different 44 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications procedures. Matching ordered events and terminal outcomes, as in WorldScapes robot and UMI pairs, preserves finer teaching relation [25]. Pairing granularity therefore determines whether the model learns an activity category, procedure, or an interaction detail. Mixed capture can reduce pairing cost. XR-2 combines 531.7 hours of robot teleoperation with roughly 1,000 hours of dual-UMI demonstrations [244]. Robot views, state, and actions supply executable targets; egocentric views and gripper motion supply candidate support. Shared laundry tasks narrow the search, while procedure-level matching identifies compatible executions. Motion-bearing demonstrations reduce correspondence uncertainty. Instrumented teaching trades restrictions on collection for less uncertainty in transfer. Handheld grippers make the demonstrators observations and motion closer to robot-compatible interface [62]. Preserving the end effector across collection and execution further reduces what must be inferred: YUBI reports 8,434 hours over 119 tasks and transfers the same gripper between arms through per-robot inverse kinematics [66]. Sharing the gripper reduces hand-to-robot correspondence uncertainty, leaving each arms reachability and control limits to be handled during execution. Bimanual teaching makes relative motion fidelity more consequential than the visual plausibility of either hand alone. Stereo-inertial tracking, synchronized views, and inter-gripper reconstruction preserve this coordination [223]. HiFi-UMIs reported 2K release also includes subtask boundaries, and its policy studies use UMI post-training without target-task teleoperation. Calibration preserves the physical relation between hands; boundaries identify which procedure that relation instantiates. Modular tracking can simplify acquisition [224], while simulation-trained whole-body controller can supply realization beyond the demonstrated gripper motion [225]. More accessible capture and more accurate coordination are consequently distinct improvements to the teaching interface. Contact sensing extends what the teaching record can express. OmniUMI synchronizes vision and motion with tactile signals, internal grasping force, and external interaction wrench [226]. Such measurements can distinguish visually similar motion performed with different contact conditions. Their transfer still depends on compatible sensing, calibration, and execution interfaces; measured wrench and commanded gripper setting carry different information. Collection can be conditioned on the current policys weaknesses. HIL-UMI compares handheld human trajectories with policy predictions on the same observation stream and targets additional data to disagreement and low-advantage segments [342]. The resulting demonstrations support further policy training. Thus policy-aware collection improves which experience is acquired, while remaining distinct from using that experience as fixed-weight deployment context. Removing the collection device shifts this burden from measurement to inference. Tracked hands and segmented point clouds can be converted into gripper poses [16]; motion inferred from human play can supply pseudo-actions, retrieved contextquery relations, and retargeted humanoid supervision [245]. These approaches broaden the usable recording pool, but the action evidence inherits reconstruction and retargeting error. The trade-off is most consequential near contact, where small positional error can change whether grasp or insertion is feasible. common action format enables joint use of these records while their reconstruction reliability determines their supervisory value. Mixed-source training can preserve this distinction instead of forcing all trajectories to carry the same supervisory weight. Aligning camera-space actions, embodiment, and chunk duration provides common temporal interface, while reliability-weighted human pseudo-actions supplement robot-supervised primary objective [246]. In ACE-Ego-0, the auxiliary objective emphasizes more dependable position channels. This weighting lets human records expand coverage while measured robot actions anchor execution. Carrying reconstruction confidence into contextual pairs likewise avoids treating uncertain hand tracking as an equally reliable robot target. Zeva-Ego separates this acquisition of physical prior from deployment adaptation [363]. Its Action-Centric Encoder converts egocentric visual transitions into continuous action-token supervision for mid-training. later interaction-conditioned stage trains the action model to use observed action effects; deployment freezes In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications Figure 16 Temporal anchors for contextual teaching: opening the door enables loading, and closing it completes the procedure. These transitions align teaching example with progress in later execution. the weights and updates memory. Human experience expands prior competence, while robot interaction supplies evidence about the current physical conditions. Motion annotation reduces the uncertainty left by ordinary video while retaining human-centered collection process. Handobject geometry [63, 64] and contemporaneous hand and finger tracking, as in EgoDexs 829 hours [65], expose motion that otherwise must be reconstructed from RGB. Robot learning still requires conversion into feasible contacts and controls. EgoScales 20,854 hours of action-labeled human data are connected to robot behavior through aligned mid-training and downstream post-training [67]; its onedemonstration experiment uses policy updates with one robot demonstration per task and additional human trajectories. These stages show why improved action evidence and fixed-weight task acquisition are separate contributions: the former can support either contextual inference or further policy fitting. The transition from human pretraining to robot deployment also changes the meaning of language supervision. Xiaomi-Robotics-1 combines over 100K hours of UMI and egocentric records with cross-embodiment posttraining [247]. State-transition descriptions during pretraining and imperative instructions during post-training serve different prediction targets. For demonstration-conditioned learning, the corresponding design choice is which task details remain unspecified by the instruction and must be recovered from the example. This connects source breadth to the pairing criterion in Section 4.2. Ordinary video broadens procedural coverage. Ordinary video reverses the trade-off of instrumented capture: activity coverage is broad, while robot-compatible action information is sparse. Egocentric activity labels help locate candidate procedures [68, 69]; paired viewpoints and short humanobject changes offer cues about correspondence and outcomes [70, 71]. These sources can identify what happened without fully specifying how different body should reproduce it. For contextual teaching, selection must preserve the choice that distinguishes this example from another clip of the same activity. Annotation is useful when it removes uncertainty about the relation teaching must preserve. Common capture protocols reduce incompatible recording conventions [248]; atomic segments and reconstructed hand and camera motion expose where an interaction begins and ends [249]. Object-state and contact annotations can resolve physical events hidden in RGB [250]. These additions are not interchangeable: reliable boundaries help preserve order, whereas contact-sensitive transfer needs relative motion and object response. The appropriate annotation follows the task distinction the support example must convey. Procedural and conversational datasets contribute another missing dimension. Assembly101 records natural variations, mistakes, and corrections during assembly and disassembly; HoloAssist pairs performers egocentric activity with an instructors spoken guidance and intervention annotations [72, 73]. Their contribution is the relationship between partial procedure and information that changes its continuation. Transferring that relationship to robot ICL requires robot-compatible continuation targets or an executor that can realize the corrected instruction. Preserving mistakes, instructions, and corrections as linked events retains this distinctive supervision. Human-video priors and demonstration following use this evidence differently. Learning latent plans from human play can reduce the robot experience needed for control [251], even when human and robot executions are not paired. Following newly supplied video additionally requires preserving the demonstrated choice in compatible robot execution. WAM-TTT learns that connection through paired humanrobot meta-training, while its deployment-time fast-weight update needs only action-free human video [11]. This is parameter 46 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications Figure 17 Reported source duration across embodied collections and general-model pretraining [58, 60, 61, 65, 67, 247, 252]. Action-aligned recordings support grounded teaching episodes; broader audiovisual corpora supply knowledge across activities and domains. The contrast motivates comparing explicit context-use training with broader pretraining. Arrowheads denote lower bounds. adaptation under the distinction in Section 2. Robot supervision establishes the connection during training; the later teaching input can omit recorded robot commands. Preserving teaching relation requires more structure than shared task name. mobile-manipulation episode contains identifiable substeps and transitions that can anchor retrieval or corrected continuation (Figure 16). Human support and robot execution can traverse those stages at different speeds, so task correspondence matters more than frame equality. Constructing this usable teaching signal incurs cost beyond recording the raw activity, motivating the acquisition comparison below.

sections.title: 4.4 Acquisition cost and contextual capability
sections.content: Data value depends on the cost of producing usable teaching, not recording alone. We first examine correspondence costs, then compare explicit contextual training with broad priors and robot grounding. Collection cost and correspondence. Filtering, synchronization, reconstruction, pairing, and validation contribute to acquisition cost. Egocentric video exposes handobject interaction; UMI also measures device motion through robot-like interface.
