The required conversion depends on the task: order-sensitive packing needs event boundaries and contrasting sequences, whereas tight insertion needs calibrated relative motion and contact evidence. Additional views or longer recordings improve coverage only if they preserve the distinctions needed for the task. Figure 17 compares source duration and evidence type. Xiaomi-Robotics-1 combines UMI and egocentric recordings; general video spans broader activity with less robot-action correspondence. Hours measure exposure, while annotation effort and usable supportquery pairs characterize the work needed to turn it into teaching. GPT-Policy makes the contribution of correspondence concrete [94]. It compares robot video with the same video augmented by aligned end-effector poses, gripper states, and commands. Plug reinsertion succeeds in zero of three video-only trials and two of three augmented-reference trials. This is combined stateaction comparison. Goal-image and occluded-goal settings provide endpoint or self-interaction evidence (Section 6), showing how the content of the acquired evidence shapes its contribution. Learning targets and acquisition routes. Pretraining can expand both executable behavior and the requirements inferred from teaching. Supportquery episodes explicitly supervise the examplecontinuation relationship [1]; GPT-3 showed that broader pretraining can also support example-based specification at In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications inference [121]. Both routes can yield fixed-parameter adaptation. Their transfer to unfamiliar rules is an empirical question distinct from the choice of training recipe. S1 and GEN-1.5 illustrate explicit contextual pairing and continuous physical experience (Section 4.2). Their shared demonstration interface motivates comparing which training relationships produced context use, with tasks, information, motor interfaces, and training budgets matched. Mechanisms of fixed-parameter context use. Fixed-parameter computations offer candidate explanations for context-dependent behavior. Bayesian accounts infer latent rule shared within sequence [318]; distributional studies identify repeated structure that favors contextual inference [111, 319]. Controlled models can bind items to labels and retrieve their association [232], or implement gradient-descent-like updates through linear self-attention [112]. Comparisons with LLaMA show that similarities between contextual and parameter learning depend on the setting [322]. These accounts distinguish what training makes inferable from the computation used at deployment. For robots, tracing taught distinction into the representation that guides action connects the training relationship to its physical consequence. General-model priors and robot grounding. Astra adds different source of prior competence to this comparison. Its public training summary describes broad text, image, and audiovisual sources, including video sources above one million hours, represented partly through transcripts, captions, or metadata [252]. In GPT-Policy, fixed general VLM interprets task references and interaction feedback, proposes robot-tool requests, and receives outcomes from constrained controller [94]. This places contextual interpretation in general model and physical realization in an explicit robot interface. The disclosure characterizes source exposure; the causal contributions of individual training components to the observed robot behavior remain unresolved. These acquisition routes supply complementary resources. Broad priors can interpret procedures and familiar interactions, while grounded records connect them to the receiving robots commands. GPT-Policys actionreference comparison illustrates this complementarity at contact-sensitive execution. The useful comparison therefore concerns the task distinctions and action correspondence obtained per unit of acquisition effort, with prior competence and the execution interface specified. From exposure to usable teaching. The reported comparisons support different conclusions: BPP varies task diversity at fixed demonstration count, S1 varies scale and prompting, and general-model disclosures describe cross-domain exposure. Together they motivate measuring the marginal value of an additional recording: does it add missing motion, distinguish another valid procedure, or reveal how to correct failure? Section 8.1 connects these contributions to selection, composition, and rule inference. Retrieval and synthesis can then target the missing relationship rather than increase volume indiscriminately.

sections.title: 4.5 Scaling data construction
sections.content: The coverage and cost analysis motivates three complementary construction routes. Retrieval reuses existing evidence; spatial supervision and task-preserving synthesis construct missing counterparts; failurecorrection collection adds continuations absent from successful demonstrations. demonstration can supply an execution reference or seed new training examples. The construction route determines which teaching relationships enter the learning units defined in Section 4.2. Autonomous collection can increase experience while changing which situations the learner encounters. Task orchestration supplies new executions [76]; learned reward and success signals can select experience for subsequent policy training [254]. contextual learner additionally needs the evidence that explains each selected continuation. Retaining its instruction, demonstration, or correction preserves candidate teaching execution pair. Contrasting pairs are needed to establish which behavior changes with that teaching. This links acquisition policy to the learning objective: selecting only successful motion favors motor competence, while preserving the preceding uncertainty and its resolution can train responsiveness to new evidence. Retrieval for training and contextual pairing. Training retrieval asks which external behavior can improve robots learned competence. Motion embeddings can locate human clips whose reconstructed trajectories provide reward guidance [255]; semantic, hand-pose, and motion similarity can select human 48 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications samples compatible with robot demonstrations [256]. In both cases, relevance is defined by the supervision entering the policys weights. This differs from contextual pairing, where the selected clip must explain particular query procedure even if both behaviors are already within the motor repertoire. PHASE selects variable-length contact phases using tactile evidence, preserving insertion-stage compatibility in the retrieved training set [411]. This supplies concrete counterpart to runtime retrieval: the selected evidence changes the policy learned offline. Pair construction has different criterion: the retrieved behavior must agree with the intended procedure. RHyME composes human clips for recorded robot trajectory through sequence-level optimal transport [80]. Existing video replaces newly captured support, but constituent behaviors must occur in both collections, and clip boundaries can introduce pairing errors. During deployment, retrieval must additionally match current progress and motion compatibility. Retrieval-based ReCAP supplies stateaction chunks to frozen residual predictor [152]; expanding that archive changes runtime context through the mechanism in Section 3. Training selection, pair construction, and runtime retrieval therefore require different judgments of relevance. Constructing spatial supervision. Spatial supervision reduces ambiguity that action loss alone must resolve. Synthetic cross-scene point correspondences associate the same task geometry across executions [161]; reconstructed contact heatmaps, hand configurations, and motion associate human interactions with affordances [176]. The first teaches where an analogous relation occurs, while the second teaches which interaction geometry is plausible. Contextual training connects either spatial prior to the supplied example, so that teaching selects which relation the robot preserves. Spatial accuracy and responsiveness to teaching then become complementary training objectives. One demonstration as reference or data seed. single demonstration can be reused as an executable reference or as seed for training data. Retrieval and alignment support the first route in MT3 [36]. The second route generates additional trajectories by preserving bimanual coordination across object-dependent changes [257, 258], or by varying reconstructed scenes and embodiments [259]. These routes place generalization in different objects: runtime reference or policy fitted to its transformed executions. For contextual training, each generated trajectory remains associated with the demonstration whose task relation it realizes. This association turns motion augmentation into supervision for interpreting new teaching. Task-preserving synthesis. Task-preserving synthesis needs both controlled variation and criterion for what remains unchanged. Randomized human-arm renderings vary embodiment appearance [260]; geometric pseudo-demonstrations and waypoint renderings construct motion-correspondent pairs [16, 77]. Executing transformed segments in simulator adds physical consequences and success filter [74]. Environment generation and compilation of task semantics into costs and transition conditions broaden the available variations [261, 262]. These operations preserve different evidence. Rendering supplies correspondence, while executed validation tests realization under modeled dynamics; contextual supervision requires both to remain tied to the governing task specification. KnowDemo makes the preserved requirement explicit [369]. It extracts task conditions from human video, grounds them in the target scene, and screens alternative contacts and subtask orders before planning and simulation. The verified trajectories then train robot policy. This connects behavioral diversity to task constraints: varying an incidental grasp can expand training coverage, while varying required order changes what the example teaches. Simulation provides controlled task and scene variation alongside executable action records. RoboCasa expanded household environments and compositional tasks in 2024; RoboCasa365 adds 365 tasks and 2,500 kitchen scenes, with 612 hours of human-operated demonstrations in simulation and 1,615 hours generated with MimicGen [75, 263]. These are simulated robot trajectories, including those collected by human operators. For ICL, the opportunity is to hold procedure fixed across environments or vary the procedure within matched environment, then verify that each generated execution preserves its assigned teaching condition. Cross-embodiment synthesis must distinguish changed appearance from newly validated interaction. Generating human-video counterparts for robot tasks starts from robot execution [24]; retargeting human motion and rendering robot arms into its scene starts from human execution [222]. In the latter, visible object responses remain those of the human recording. Physical-consistency and forwardinverse checks can 49 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications test whether converted transition admits compatible action [264, 265]. The teaching relation adds another requirement: the conversion must preserve order, goal, and binding contacts. physically plausible transition can still be the wrong continuation for the supplied demonstration. Agent collection can obtain additional executions through shared interfaces. GUMI records pre-action observations and semantic commands for humans and agents [31]. An ICL collection could use this interface to execute contrasting valid orders in comparable scenes, retaining each task specification, recording, and outcome. Pairing each successful execution with its governing specification would preserve the distinction needed for contextual supervision. Processing must preserve intentional variation. An AgiBot-based study finds that demonstrator-specific speed variation can assign different chunks to similar observations, and that reducing this ambiguity improves downstream learning [266]. Uniform speed conversion is unsuitable when insertion requires alignment phases or pouring requires pauses. The corresponding ICL decision is selective: normalize incidental collection style while retaining pause, route, or contact order when it is part of what the example teaches. Failurecorrection collection. Successful demonstrations leave recovery states underrepresented. Corrective collection changes the state distribution on which supervision is obtained: DAgger queries an expert on learnervisited states [267], DART uses perturbations to elicit nearby corrections [268], and selective intervention concentrates human effort [269]. XR-2s separation of policy actions from human takeovers improves folding from 58% to 93% across three retraining rounds [244]. This expands the repairs represented in weights. Contextual recovery requires retaining the linked failure and feedback as well, so the learner can infer which repair the current evidence calls for. The source of correction determines what can be learned about its applicability. Synthetic perturbations, intervention in predicted rollouts, and planner-guided exploration expose different failure continuations [270 272]. Learning from intervention and autonomous outcomes can use these records without imitating every action [273]. For contextual learning, the record must retain the relation among the failed action, the corrective change, and its consequence. Action-level arguments and return values make that relation more specific than task-level failure flag, as ASPIRE illustrates [47]. Richer failure records are useful when they help distinguish the causes later correction must address. Corrective records also need to expose mistaken task-state estimates. After failed grasp, the gripper may be empty while stored plan marks pickup complete. Linking the repair to observations that establish this discrepancy supplies supervision for revising context as well as motion. Retaining the repair as guidance changes the external artifacts Bn in Equation (19); using its trajectories as policy targets changes neural parameters. Section 7 tests whether either acquisition improves later tasks.

sections.title: 4.6 Connecting teaching data to a pretrained policy
sections.content: Data construction must be matched by an interface through which teaching can change behavior. Three dependencies organize this integration: access to the evidence, preservation of its task distinction in the control intermediate, and an action encoding that can realize it. Access comes first. An observation-conditioned policy such as ACT needs an added context channel to distinguish procedures compatible with the same scene [274]. Language-conditioned policies expose goals and constraints [118, 119]; goal images specify endpoints [275]; sequential demonstrations can supply order or contact preferences [13, 55]. Adding an encoder provides access, while teaching-dependent targets establish use. The missing dependency determines which training records method needs. Foundation policies supply perception and motor interfaces [118, 275279], but the four families consume different task-specific intermediates: actions, geometric references, futures, or executable specifications. Subtask annotations and skill representations expose higher-level structure [30, 60, 61, 241]; phase-aligned examples connect that structure to current decision [18]. Direct supervision of an intermediate is one way to establish this connection. Joint training, pretrained interpretation, and geometric construction can also supply it. The requirement shared by the four interfaces is that the execution intermediate preserve the distinction selected by the evidence. 50 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications Human pretraining and deployment teaching act at different stages of this connection. Richer robot pretraining can increase the benefit of joint fine-tuning on human and robot demonstrations with reconstructed motion and subtask labels [280]. For ICL, the resulting policy must additionally respond to new example with its parameters fixed. Conditioning on language, quality, speed, control modality, and visual subgoals, as in the π0.7 recipe [281], illustrates how inputs can distinguish otherwise mixed executions. Demonstration conditioning can extend these inputs when video conveys the distinction that the action generator needs. Encoding is the final bottleneck between an informative training pair and an executable command. Regularized ICRT action tokens and hierarchical tokenization preserve different aspects of motion [282, 283]. LipVQ-VAEs improvement from low robot-success baseline shows that relieving representation bottleneck can help while leaving execution difficult. The teaching signal passes through successive constraints: pairing identifies the intended relation, context encoding retains it, and action representation makes its realization expressible. These three stages must preserve the same taught distinction. The next chapter follows that requirement into deployment, where the current physical state determines how it can be realized and revised after failure. Takeaways ① Data sources determine the available measurements; teachingexecution relationships determine what context can teach. Robot data supports motor competence; alternative taught behaviors within the same scene expose the additional dependence on demonstrations. ② Retrieval can select training data, construct demonstrationexecution pair, or supply examples during control. Only the last directly changes frozen policys input at deployment; the first two change the experience from which it learns. ③ Useful scaling adds missing motor competence, task-defining alternatives, or evidence that changes later attempt. The value of added experience follows the new distinctions it makes available to the learner.

sections.title: 5 Grounding: How Does Context Guide Recovery?
sections.content: Objects can move, grasps can fail, and resistance can change after task has been correctly interpreted. Recovery aims to preserve the taught requirement while revising the state estimate and continuation. It establishes the current state, diagnoses the deviation, and selects feasible repair. Retaining the repair with its applicable conditions makes that feedback useful beyond the current attempt.

sections.title: 5.1 Grounding the task in the current physical state
sections.content: Grounding requires two complementary estimates: the task requirement that remains binding and the physical state that may have changed. An insertion can preserve its destination and prerequisite order despite moved part. We establish these estimates before examining motion feasibility and the entry conditions of transferred segments. Preserving the task reference during execution. transferable task reference must distinguish progress toward goal from adherence to the taught procedure. Cross-view progress representations can align executions despite appearance or embodiment changes [78, 79]; demonstration-conditioned skill inference selects which procedure that progress belongs to [29, 80]. Current observations must then establish whether its prerequisites occurred and its required contacts remain valid. Terminal appearance can conceal an incorrect order, so verification must use the relations supplied by teaching [284]. This connects correspondence in Section 3.5 to recovery: deviation is meaningful only relative to the procedure the robot was actually asked to follow. Figure 18 distinguishes three failures in video-conditioned manipulation. An occluded interaction calls for view that restores the missing geometry; lost grasp calls for checking contact before resuming transport; wrong target calls for revisiting the instruction and demonstration correspondence. Each repair addresses different missing fact. Contact-intensive tasks add another ambiguity: stalled insertion can reflect misalignment, unfamiliar resistance, or excessive force. bounded probe can distinguish physical responses, whereas an irreversible operation may require inspection or clarification before another attempt. 51 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications Figure 18 Three failures call for different recovery evidence: (a) visual occlusion, (b) grasp loss, and (c) incorrect target selection. Human demonstrations on the left establish the intended behavior; robot executions on the right reveal where realization departs from it. Maintaining current, task-relevant scene. repair must distinguish an intended change from its observed outcome. placement command or predicted future specifies what should happen; completion evidence supports recording the step as finished. If the part subsequently moves, its remembered pose needs revision while the earlier placement instruction can remain binding. Memory and geometry-indexed retrieval recover unavailable observations [285, 286]; dynamic scene records replace spatial facts contradicted by new measurements [287289]. When neither establishes applicability, another view or reversible probe can distinguish the remaining explanations [290, 291]. navigation failure can similarly invalidate remembered route or its terrain assessment. VLM-GroNav [353] aligns visual terrain examples with sinkage or slip indicators before revising traversal estimates. This distinguishes physical feedback about surface from geometric evidence that passage is open. Applicability can be checked before remembered event influences control. CoreSense examines episode scope, provenance, temporal validity, and consistency [343]. Its recorded-data and simulated-signal evaluation measures evidence selection. Physical recovery evaluates the subsequent step: whether the selected evidence supports repair that succeeds on the robot. Connecting intended change to feasible motion. corrected interpretation needs an executable continuation. Forwardinverse consistency checks agreement between proposed actions and modeled transitions; force-conditioned control adds measured contact feedback [265, 292]. These mechanisms make contextselected correction executable. When the required motion lies outside the controllers repertoire, recovery also requires new skill or change in the physical setup. Checking whether transferred segment still applies. Geometric one-shot methods distinguish initial alignment from recovery during execution. DOME and ODIL first establish relative starting configuration, whereas staged alignment can re-establish it at later subtask boundaries [33, 37, 177]. transport segment also depends on the object remaining grasped: after slip, geometric alignment can persist while the segments entry condition fails. Its entry condition and intended completion therefore carry different information: the former establishes whether the recorded motion can begin, and the latter whether the next segment should follow. Learned subgoal transitions similarly govern progression within trained long-horizon policies [293]. Failure can invalidate reference or expose missing control competence. Robustness via Retrying recomputes continuation through image registration and predictive control [294]; ScrewMimic uses demonstrated In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications screw-motion representation to guide further bimanual learning [295]. The former changes the continuation through existing components; the latter improves the component that realizes it. This distinction directs recovery toward revising the current reference or expanding the motor capability needed to realize it.

sections.title: 5.2 From failure evidence to corrective execution
sections.content: Recovery proceeds from assessment to diagnosis and correction. Assessment establishes deviation from the taught procedure; diagnostic evidence distinguishes its plausible causes; the controllers correction interface determines which repair can be executed. The resulting continuation may be absent from the successful demonstration. Task-conditioned progress assessment. Failure assessment requires reference for what should have happened. Action consistency, visual progress, and calibrated rollout scores can detect departures from expected execution [81, 82, 296]. For ICL, the reference follows the current teaching, allowing an unfamiliar but valid order to define expected progress. GVL illustrates example-conditioned assessment by using observation progress examples to improve frozen VLMs estimates from shuffled frames, including human examples for robot trajectories [83]. The taught reference makes progress assessment responsive to the current task. Progress and physical acceptability can disagree. connector can reach its apparent destination with an unsuitable contact force, just as kit can reach the right inventory in the wrong order. Verification must therefore test both the context-defined requirement and the measurements needed to establish acceptable execution. Diagnostic evidence acquisition. Diagnosis turns failure detection into repair choice by identifying the likely cause. Multisensory diagnosis and learned failure knowledge organize clues to stalled action [84, 85], but misalignment and an unseen obstruction can still require different interventions. Uncertainty about the intended task can be reduced by clarification and reasoning over alternative plans [86, 297, 298]. Uncertainty about resistance instead requires sensing or interaction, including tactile evidence absent from RGB [299]. The unresolved cause determines the information source: teaching clarifies intent, while sensed action effects reveal the resistance encountered by the robot. Task-context exploration and question-based teaching formalize the choice to acquire evidence [300, 301]. The useful check is the one that discriminates causes relevant to the next action: view for occlusion, contact feedback for grasp loss, or clarification for ambiguous intent. Affordance Agent Harness routes detection, segmentation, and other skills, verifies evidence, and retries before committing an actionable region [376]. Its episodic memory supplies priors for recurring objects. This illustrates how verification can govern evidence acquisition before motion controller uses the result. Correction granularity and feasibility. Correction granularity should match the cause of failure. wrong target requires changing task selection; displaced approach point requires spatial update; insufficient displacement may require only magnitude adjustment. Corrective-language training makes supervisory instructions actionable [87], while sparse adjustments around frozen VLA can address magnitude errors when the target is already correct [142]. Subtask, motion, and pixel-target interfaces expose these changes at different resolutions [210]. The controller must also accept the correction from the state already reached, connecting diagnostic precision to the steerability analysis in Section 3. Iterative in-context policy improvement links an observed error directly to motion primitives settings. frozen language model uses primitive parameters, execution errors, and correction examples to propose an adjustment; its comparison favors relative errors over raw states and targets [9]. The error is useful because it identifies change the primitive can make. Neural parameters stay fixed, while the generated control settings change within the primitives available range. When the frozen action policy cannot continue from the failure state, CoRe uses history and counterfactual continuations to choose rejoin state, then realigns displaced objects before returning control [302]. The teaching still specifies the task; restoration makes an existing skill usable again. Recovery can instead revise the history that conditions prediction. FARE compares full causal cache, recovered prefix, and reset cache under the same latest observation, selecting their predicted continuations 53 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications Table 12 How teaching and feedback support assessment, correction, and reuse. Each row links supplied evidence to the decision or control element it changes. ENPIRE denotes its program-refinement branch. Work Assessment and assistance GVL [83] IntroPlan [298] Available evidence Observationprogress examples Retrieved reasoning examples Affected output Progress estimate Plan; clarification Corrective execution ICPI [9] RACER [87] CorrectVLA [142] Experience reuse DROC [46] Zeva [88] ENPIRE [89] Execution errors; correction examples Current images; corrective language Human feedback Motion-primitive parameters Action continuation Sparse action bias Retrieved language corrections Actioneffect history Execution feedback Plan; skill calls Subsequent actions Executable program with frozen world-action model [402]. This changes the models retained evidence rather than physically restoring the scene. compatible historical prefix must therefore be re-grounded in the current state. Its ablations find that always invoking recovery search or committing an unverified prefix can underperform the base policy, supporting selective intervention with verification. continuation must also preserve completed steps and restore failed prerequisites, as captured by task graphs and verified subgoal memory [206, 303]. Feedback is useful when it identifies decision the robot can revise: its estimate of progress, its next action, or rule retained for later use  (Table 12)  . contextual repair must change that decision while preserving the task requirements outside the corrections scope. This connects immediate recovery to the longer-term validity of the lesson it produces.

sections.title: 5.3 Applicability and reuse of corrections
sections.content: Reuse retains conditional lesson: which intervention corrected which failure, and under what conditions. Guidance or executable artifacts preserve it through Equation (19); corrective training can incorporate such lessons into policy weights (Section 4). Different lessons require different reset rules. Language-correction memory retains task constraints, whereas actioneffect history retains physical response [46, 88]. workcell reset clears completed-step memory; changed connector or tool can invalidate response estimate while leaving the assembly order intact. For jammed connector, an adjustment justified by measured resistance should not be reused when misalignment is the cause. Retaining the observation, intervention, and outcome allows later attempts to reassess that condition instead of replaying the repair unconditionally. Program-based reuse makes repairs executable. ENPIREs program-revision branch uses fixed neural models; Zetta retains critics and recovery routines around frozen policy [89, 90]. Interruptible execution exposes intervention points [304]. Later trials test the repairs benefit under applicable conditions. Task structure and irreversibility determine what can be repeated, linking recovery to the application demands below. Takeaways ① Context specifies the recovery reference and helps interpret failure. Physical measurements establish quality; responsive control interface makes the correction executable. ② Corrective training expands available repairs; contextual recovery selects or revises one from fresh evidence. Reuse requires retaining the correction with its outcome and applicable physical conditions.

sections.title: 6 Applications: What Must Context Resolve?
sections.content: The value of context depends on the uncertainty an application makes consequential. Manipulation can leave the intended interaction unspecified; navigation can hide the route or local spatial structure; long procedure 54 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications Figure 19 Cross-embodiment skill transfer in UniSkill [30]: (a) tissue pulling, (b) lid closing, and (c) cloth placement. Human demonstrations above and robot executions below preserve the interaction despite changes in embodiment and object appearance. can hide completed prerequisite; an unfamiliar body can hide its response to action. These demands determine what teaching, observation, or interaction must supply. Repeated task changeover combines them with acquisition and reuse costs. Any of the four method families can serve several demands, provided its intermediate preserves the information the application requires.

sections.title: 6.1 Task specification in manipulation
sections.content: In rearrangement, an instruction or demonstration can specify which object belongs in which container, how components should be ordered, or which tool serves purpose. moved destination requires new path that preserves the demonstrated objectdestination relation. The Imitator Game makes differences between demonstration and execution explicit through scene, object, and functional changes [101]. These changes test preservation of intent across altered object correspondence. We first consider the distinctions an example must convey, then how they survive replacement of the objects involved, and finally how geometry or contact response changes their realization. When an example conveys more than task label. The value of demonstration depends on what the user needs to specify. final drawing leaves stroke order, direction, and tool approach unresolved; BPPs DrawAnything study connects broader drawing-task diversity to better demonstration-conditioned generalization [54]. In its three-task laundry study, language is more reliable than behavior demonstrations, with some demonstration-conditioned failures executing the wrong fold. These contrasting settings identify an application condition: video is especially useful when it communicates choice that short task label or goal image leaves open. goal image can specify the task when only visible endpoint matters; demonstration additionally conveys required path or order. Replacing objects makes the distinction between task meaning and execution concrete. new workpiece can preserve an assembly relation while changing its grasp; new fixture can preserve the goal while changing the insertion geometry. Replacing both requires correspondence at both ends of the interaction, as the object-pair transfers in Section 3.5 illustrate. The application must specify whether an object identity is binding or whether another object may serve the same role. Functional substitution is useful only when it preserves that requirement, including contact, order, and material constraints. 55 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications Figure 20 Task meaning and physical realization vary independently: (a) an unchanged baseline, (b) new task relation, (c) changed physical response, and (d) both changes together. Teaching specifies the intended relation; interaction reveals how the robot can realize it. Personalized behavior adds persistent conventions to task specification. Language corrections can retain user preferences and guide subsequent plans [46, 305]. request to place objects quietly should govern later placements, whereas correction to one objects location need not. Such applications require both an acceptable endpoint and adherence to the users continuing constraint. Realizing these requirements across bodies adds correspondence problem. In bimanual transfer, coordination must be preserved while each arm uses feasible motion. Conditioning one predicted arm trajectory on the other addresses dependence within the action inference problem [92]. Sharing an end effector across arms reduces different uncertainty, the physical mismatch between demonstration and execution [66]. Teaching specifies the intended cloth region or contact relation; action inference and embodiment design determine how coordinated motion realizes it. Figure 19 shows the preserved interaction across human and robot executions: pulling tissue, closing lid, or placing cloth. The relevant object part and destination remain identifiable while the robot changes its approach and contacts. handle-specific instruction restricts that variation; an endpoint-only request leaves the grasp open. Method selection follows the binding requirement. Geometric transfer exposes contact or motion constraint; skill interface exposes order and prerequisites; contextual policies and predictive control can encode either through their learned intermediates. The application supplies the criterion for judging these choices. Training pairs that equate executions solely by endpoint can erase route or contact requirement that the user values (Section 4.2). When intent and physical response change together. Deformable manipulation couples the procedure to changing scene. fold alters visible surfaces and accessible contacts, so the correct next action cannot be obtained by repeatedly matching the initial demonstration frame. Geometric and semantic information can jointly condition folding policy [91]; preserving fold boundaries then provides more useful correspondence than copying absolute hand trajectories. Instant-Folds simulated mode variation and real garment variation examine different parts of this transfer. Its RGB-D and interaction interface, including estimated and potentially corrected human interaction points, also supplies richer information than ordinary RGB demonstration video. Material changes can leave the intended fold unchanged while altering the force needed to realize it. Visuotactile measurements distinguish completion from excessive compression [306]. Here the demonstration 56 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications supplies the procedure and actioneffect evidence supplies the current material response, giving the two context sources different roles. new arrangement under familiar conditions primarily changes the requested relation. familiar insertion under changed resistance primarily changes physical realization. new fold on unfamiliar fabric couples both: the taught fold remains the reference, but each action alters the geometry and contact conditions for the next. This independent variation provides basis for choosing teaching and feedback, even within one application. Figure 20 crosses the two demands: changed task relation, changed physical response, or both. This view identifies what evidence an application needs before comparing the method used to process it. Navigation extends this question from object interaction to spatial knowledge and traversability.

sections.title: 6.2 Navigation and spatial adaptation
sections.content: Navigation requires more than destination: robot may need demonstrated route, knowledge of an unfamiliar building, examples of how to interpret directions, or feedback about an unsuccessful passage. Table 13 organizes this evidence into four context types. The following paragraphs compare them in parallel by what they convey and how they change navigation. This application taxonomy concerns the supplied information; the method families in Section 3 concern the computation that turns it into behavior. Several context types can be used together. Table 13 Navigation contexts grouped by the information they supply at deployment. Each type supports distinct decision, and system can combine several types. These information categories complement the four computational method families in Section 3. Context type Evidence and decision Representative approaches Route demonstrations Ordered views or landmarks, sometimes with actions. Follow demonstrated path or sequence of subgoals. Zero-Shot Visual Imitation [355]; RPF [356]; sparse visual memory [357] Environment observations Instruction and decision examples Outcome feedback Scene previews or earlier visits. Locate objects and connecting passages for new goals. SPTM [358]; NOLO [351]; ReLIC [203]; NavProbe [383]; SparseNav [396] Instructionlandmark, instructionsubtask, or imagedecision pairs. Interpret new instruction or select move. LM-Nav [359]; A2Nav [360]; Select2Plan [352] Outcomes, failure notes, terrain response, or corrective dialogue. Revise guidance or traversal costs. VLM-GroNav [353]; CMMR-VLN [361]; HAM-VLN [362]; Talk2Escape [384] Route demonstrations specify where to go in sequence. tour can teach particular passage through an environment: pass the reception desk, traverse corridor, and stop by the stairs. The ordered reference remains relevant even when execution deviates from the original camera poses. Zero-Shot Visual Imitation [355] treats demonstration images as successive goals for pretrained goal-conditioned policy, including navigation with TurtleBot in unseen offices. RPF [356] instead encodes views and recorded actions into path memory that guides execution under motion noise and scene changes. Sparse visual memory [357] reduces the retained views while preserving the action sequence, examining how much visual evidence path following needs. These approaches differ in whether the reference specifies visual subgoals or an action-bearing route. Their shared mechanism aligns present progress with the demonstrated route. Environment observations reveal where places and objects are. preview or earlier visit can reveal the building without prescribing the next route. SPTM [358] converts an exploration recording into graph of visual locations, then selects reachable waypoints for different goals using fixed retrieval and control networks. NOLO [351] conditions navigation actions on scene video, while ReLIC [203] accumulates experience across episodes with changing starts and goals in one home. NavProbe uses spatial index to find visual and geometric evidence relevant to the current subgoal [383]. Its executive consults these records when the available evidence is insufficient, then revises the subgoal before invoking navigation skills. The distinction is 57 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications how local knowledge becomes available: graph, supplied sequence, policy memory, or actively retrieved evidence. new goal can reuse these facts; new building requires acquiring them again. CLUE additionally lets exploration revise what the task requires: hypotheses about relevant objects and functions are tested against an online language-embedded map [406]. Context acquisition then resolves an underspecified objective as well as an unknown route. The current instruction can also decide which facts are worth acquiring. SparseNav retains traversability geometry but grounds semantic landmarks only when the active sub-instruction makes their location useful [396]. Its sparse landmark memory and instruction-progress record then guide waypoint selection. This separates maintaining navigable map from repeatedly labeling every visible object. Together with NavProbes targeted retrieval, it treats context construction as decision about missing information. The resulting context is organized around the active instruction and the evidence needed for its next navigation decision. Instruction and decision examples teach an interpretation. Example pairs can specify how navigation request should be translated into executable choices. LM-Nav [359] supplies instructionlandmark examples to language model; the extracted sequence is grounded in topological graph and executed by pretrained navigator. A2Nav [360] extends this interpretation to action demands: passing doorway and entering it require different subtasks even when the landmark is identical. Its prompted parser selects among navigators trained for these demands. Select2Plan [352] moves example conditioning closer to the decision itself by retrieving imageanswer pairs for movement or waypoint selection. Thus the example can teach symbolic decomposition or visual choice. Unlike route recording tied to particular places, such pairing can explain how to interpret new query using an existing execution interface. Outcome feedback revises what should be attempted next. Execution adds evidence that successful demonstration may omit: branch was unhelpful, stopping decision was premature, or visually open surface caused slip. CMMR-VLN [361] stores successful routes and notes about the first incorrect decision for retrieval in later navigation. HAM-VLN [362] attaches failure notes to visited places during an episode, making them available when those regions become relevant again. VLM-GroNav [353] grounds terrain judgments in physical interaction and updates waypoint selection and local traversal costs. Talk2Escape acquires additional guidance when retained evidence cannot resolve failure: detected looping or trajectory divergence triggers landmark-grounded question to human or oracle [384]. The reply corrects navigation context. Feedback thus revises decision through remembered outcomes, physical measurements, or newly requested clarification. These lessons remain useful while the associated instruction, place, and physical conditions still apply. The four navigation contexts retain different things: prescribed route, facts about an environment, an interpretation rule, or conditional lesson. Their validity therefore changes at different boundaries. new goal can reuse map but replace the route; new building invalidates local locations while leaving an interpretation convention useful; changed terrain can invalidate an earlier traversal estimate. Section 7.1 translates these distinctions into controls. Combining navigation with manipulation adds procedural state: after reaching pickup site, the robot must establish whether the object was acquired. The next subsection examines these dependencies across complete procedure.

sections.title: 6.3 Long procedures and irreversible operations
sections.content: Long procedures change the teaching problem from selecting an action to maintaining dependency structure. Interaction phases and sequential end-effector goals can expose it explicitly, including in teleoperated RGB-D demonstration interfaces [93]; context-conditioned policy must retain the corresponding distinctions in its representation. An unfinished step, completed step, and failed prerequisite require different continuations even when the current image is similar. Long procedures therefore require correspondence between the teachers successful sequence and the robots interrupted or incomplete execution, beyond retaining longer record. The analysis moves from dependency tracking to the additional constraints imposed by irreversible steps. Irreversible procedures add constraint on how progress and failure can be established. In laboratory workflows, intermediate products must remain valid while the robot decides how to continue. Benchmarks spanning atomic skills, compositions, and extended workflows expose the interaction of procedural inference 58 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications Figure 21 Three decision roles of context: (a) task specification selects the object and destination; (b) interaction guidance conveys how the cloth should move onto the plate; (c) execution-state tracking uses the result of removing the towel to advance from uncovering the target to placing the lemon. Representative implementations are VIMA [100], UniSkill [30], and GPT-Policy [94], respectively. and dexterity [95]; household planning with low-level embodiment abstracted away isolates dependencies among steps [307]. Varying the supplied procedure within these settings would test whether contextual teaching preserves dependencies through the available executor. Long procedures also couple memories with different validity periods. Progress memory records which steps have been completed; physical memory estimates how to perform the remaining operation. Zevas two-timescale analysis tests reuse of action effects across reset attempts [88]. In laboratory workflow, however, physical reset may be impossible: repeating an insertion and repeating dose have different consequences. The informative next interaction must therefore respect both the taught dependency structure and the state of the intermediate product. Reversibility determines how the recovery mechanisms in Section 5 can be used. placement may permit local correction; dispensing or fastening can require inspection before retry. The application therefore needs evidence of completed operations, alongside the demonstrated dependency structure, to decide whether failed step can be resumed. The distinctions in Figure 21 concern what information is missing from the next decision. In (a), task specification identifies the required objectdestination relation among alternatives already present in the scene. In (b), interaction guidance conveys the motion relation that should survive the change from human hand to robot gripper. In (c), execution-state tracking establishes that the plate has been uncovered, making lemon placement the next feasible step [94]. These examples instantiate the information roles in Section 2: panel (b) combines specified interaction with cross-embodiment correspondence, while panel (c) updates execution state under an unchanged goal. They are complementary information requirements within task, and can be supplied together through language, demonstrations, and interaction history. new procedure can require either new arrangement of available operations or motion the current policy has not acquired. Assembly adaptation through fast weights [10] and GEN-1.5s brush-to-dustpan example after five minutes of fine-tuning [98] place new evidence into parameters. They provide useful comparison with fixed-weight teaching: context can select, order, and parameterize available operations, including new motions within the executors capabilities; further policy learning can expand those capabilities. This separation localizes long-procedure failures to task interpretation or motor competence. 59 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications Long-procedure evaluation must separate adherence to new ordering from adaptation to changed physical response. Body and dynamics adaptation isolates the second demand: how familiar requirement is realized when the physical system changes.

sections.title: 6.4 Adaptation to body and dynamics
sections.content: Body adaptation isolates physical response while keeping the requested task specified. Locomotion makes this separation explicit; manipulation introduces analogous uncertainty through payloads and contact. Their combination in mobile manipulation then requires procedure and progress memory alongside the physical estimate. direction or speed command can already specify the goal; recent action consequences reveal how the current body and terrain respond. Learned adaptation modules address this physical uncertainty [39], while longer-context experience broadens the setting toward different morphologies, actuator changes, and evidence retained across attempts [40]. broader range of bodies expands the response variations that the policy must infer from its interaction history. Locomotion also separates change in the requested behavior from change in the body that realizes it. Example-conditioned foot-contact generation can specify gait-like procedure for pretrained controller [96]. Active tracking across wheeled, quadrupedal, and aerial platforms instead uses shared velocity interface, with body-specific realization delegated to lower-level control and visual history identifying the moving target [97]. The shared interface supports cross-platform execution by assigning target tracking to visual history and body-specific motion to lower-level control. The contextual contribution depends on whether the evidence specifies gait, tracks target, or identifies an unfamiliar response. Manipulation introduces analogous uncertainty through new gripper, payload, or deformable object. RopeFormer retains actionresponse history across trials on unseen ropes, adapting rotation and whipping with fixed policy weights [364]. MetaPusher instead updates dynamics model during pushing and revises the plan for the unfamiliar object [368]. The goal can remain fixed in both cases: interaction reveals how to realize it under changed physical conditions. Combining this evidence with demonstrations requires distinguishing changed task requirement from changed response. Histories of stable command under different body or terrain responses provide the training relationship for this adaptation. Mobile manipulation combines this requirement with procedural teaching and the spatial knowledge discussed in Section 6.2. In delivery procedure, the example specifies the destination and handling order, lifting an object changes the payload, and execution memory records whether pickup has completed. The contextual learner must retain the procedure and progress while updating the physical estimate as the load changes. Evaluating the combination requires both adherence to the demonstrated handling and reliable transport under the changed response. Procedural teaching and response adaptation become especially valuable when the same capabilities serve recurring tasks. Their practical benefit then depends on which acquired knowledge can be reused and which conditions must be checked again.

sections.title: 6.5 Task changeover, teaching, and reuse
sections.content: Frequent procedural change over reusable motor repertoire gives contextual teaching concrete application. Two kitting orders can use the same parts and grasps but require different placement sequences or handling conventions. demonstration is useful when it communicates that difference beyond the bill of materials; shorter instruction can suffice for fully specified count or destination. Across batches, the chosen sequence persists while completed-step memory resets. changed tool requires new physical estimate while the order may remain valid. This separates three parts of changeover: specifying what changes, acquiring the evidence needed to validate it, and retaining the result for subsequent batches. The recurring change determines the economical teaching channel. Counts or destinations may be stated directly; fold can require sequential example; changed material may require test interaction. Precision and irreversibility determine the verification needed before accepting the new procedure (Section 5). Changeover therefore measures the complete acquisition process, including the evidence needed to validate it. 60 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications Table 14 Teaching and reuse interfaces relevant to production. GEN-1.5, S1, and GLOW condition execution with fixed weights; physical feedback can instead revise programs or train policies. System Task evidence Adaptation Context or artifact Demonstrations condition robot execution GEN-1.5 [98] Sensors; trajectories Physical prompting Demonstration; history S1 [99] Video demonstration Video conditioning Demonstration GLOW [389] Single human video Contextual action generation Encoded skill context HOST [23] Human video; robot progress Predict; decode Demonstration Physical feedback revises procedures and learning experiments ASPIRE [47] Task; execution traces Diagnose; repair Repair guidance ENPIRE [89] Task; physical trial outcomes Revise code; train policy Programs; policies The relevant endpoint is repeatable execution at the required quality. Reusing task specification can reduce preparation for later batches, while changed tools or materials create new validation cost. This distinguishes the value of contextual teaching at changeover from the value of retained procedure during production. Section 7.4 measures both through teaching, interaction, and operating effort. Teaching and reuse interfaces. Teaching can specify task for existing competence or revise the resources used in later execution  (Table 14)  . Sensorimotor and video prompts specify tasks without retraining [98, 99]; HOST instead predicts task evolution before decoding actions [23]. GLOW reports watering and box-storage examples that reuse encoded skill context across changed objects or positions [389]. The qualitative cases illustrate reuse of supplied teaching, while aggregate benchmark scores summarize broader capability. Context interventions isolate the demonstrations contribution (Section 7.1). Outcome-driven reuse changes what is retained. ASPIRE preserves repair guidance [47]; ENPIRE can revise control program or train policy [89]. Prompt preparation, physical trials, and training incur different changeover costs. Their value depends on whether the change requires another procedure, correction of recurring failure, or motion outside existing competence. The next chapter evaluates these contributions to task acquisition and reuse. Takeaways ① Applications determine the missing information: an object relation, spatial knowledge, procedural state, or physical response. Each requires teaching or feedback that resolves the corresponding uncertainty. ② Unclear requirements call for teaching; uncertain execution conditions call teraction; missing motor competence calls for an expanded executor or additional skill These deficits require different remedies. for observation or inlearning. ③ Task changes create value for new teaching; repeated operations create value for retained procedures. Acquisition and verification costs determine that value, especially when actions are irreversible or time-critical.

sections.title: 7 Evaluation: When Does Context Help?
sections.content: Evaluation traces the contribution of context from changed evidence to physical success. Familiar scenes, executor capabilities, and retry opportunities provide the comparison conditions needed to isolate that contribution. Does changed evidence produce the appropriate change in behavior? Does that change survive physical execution and transfer? Does retaining the lesson improve later attempt enough to justify its acquisition cost? Context interventions, intermediate diagnostics, and retention tests separate these questions. Reported comparisons ground the analysis; proposed controls test the learning mechanisms behind them. 61 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications Figure 22 Two tests of contextual transfer. (a) Changing the demonstration while holding the robot scene fixed changes UniSkill's predicted continuation [30]. (b) LIBERO-PRO changes objects to test target selection [106]. Together, these axes motivate tests that vary teaching and object identity independently, measuring both the inferred requirement and its physical realization.

sections.title: 7.1 Context use and transfer across tasks and environments
sections.content: Context interventions test sensitivity to teaching; changes in tasks, objects, environments, or bodies locate its transfer boundary. Varying evidence quantity, retention distance, and distractors tests access to the required information. Sensitivity to task-defining context. Demonstrations specifying different feasible behaviors in the same robot scene isolate the influence of teaching. In kitting task, changing the demonstrated part count should change the selected count; changing the demonstrator while preserving that count should preserve the requirement. Together, meaning-changing and meaning-preserving interventions test what information the learner uses. Success without context provides the prior-only comparison. fully specified target tests whether the required behavior is executable. Instruction benchmarks illustrate why these controls matter. LIBERO varies spatial, object, goal, and procedural factors [228], yet task-index embeddings can achieve high performance when the scene reveals task identity [309]. LIBERO-CF supplies alternative feasible instructions within familiar layouts and finds that tested VLAs often continue the scene-associated task [107]. For demonstration ICL, replacing video must therefore change the intended order or relation, rather than merely perturb its appearance. Robustness tests supply the complementary invariant: preserve the required procedure across viewpoint, object appearance, or instruction rephrasing [106, 310]. RoboStressBench separates material, viewpoint, lighting, and geometry stresses to diagnose upstream visual recognition, reasoning, and planning [377]. VidPair-Halluc instead pairs similar backgrounds with different foreground semantics [378]. Applied to demonstration evaluation, this design would test whether inferred task content follows the demonstrated event rather than scene similarity; subsequent rollout tests physical realization. Show-Harnesss video-order comparison provides task information left unspecified by the no-video instruction [31]. An equally informative textual order is the relevant control for claim about videos particular advantage. Comparing language-only, demonstration-only, and joint context with matched task information separates modality from information content. Holding the instruction fixed while changing the demonstrated convention tests learning from examples; holding the demonstration fixed while changing correction tests use of feedback. Discovering an unfamiliar action convention proved harder: without supplied conventions, the system succeeds in one of 20 episodes and infers 23.3% of mappings correctly. Interpreting demonstrated procedure and discovering an unfamiliar action interface thus require separate evidence. 62 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications Table 15 Proposed evaluation controls and resources that illustrate the corresponding capabilities. Comparisons hold other task conditions fixed; cross-attempt tests separate physical resets from memory resets. Capability Context use Intervention Change teaching Readout Example resources Task-consistent actions Relation transfer Hold out relations Relation adherence Evidence retention Retain or clear history Recall; memory updates Cross-attempt reuse Separate reset types Gain; interference Physical transfer Change dynamics Adaptation; goal fidelity Human-data transfer Scene robustness Vary human data; fix robot data Change scene Trained-policy success Target; outcome Execution steering Physical execution Change command Supply target or prerequisites Target selection; success Redirection; success Route teaching Change route; retain goal Spatial adaptation Change preview; reset memory Example interpretation Change examples; retain Path; landmark-order adherence Success; route efficiency Outcome reuse query Remove notes; retain retries Repeated errors; path cost Parsed subtasks; selected moves LIBERO-CF [107]; LMAct [102] VIMA [100]; MOSAIC [12]; Imitator Game [101] RoboMME [103]; MEMOBench [104] RopeFormer [364]; Zeva-Ego [363] MemMimic [105]; PACE-Bench [308] H2RBench [366] LIBERO [228]; LIBERO-PRO [106] ReSteer [108] RoboSemanticBench [109]; Behavior-Skill [110] RPF [356]; sparse visual memory [357] NOLO [351]; ReLIC [203] A2Nav [360]; Select2Plan [352] CMMR-VLN [361]; HAM-VLN [362] Traversability Withhold terrain feedback Success; physical disturbance VLM-GroNav [353] Sensitivity to teaching and robustness of execution require different observations. changed predicted continuation can expose changed task interpretation; rollout establishes whether the robot realizes it. UniSkills decoded futures and LIBERO-PROs object substitutions illustrate these complementary views (Figure 22). The former diagnoses an inferred skill within skilland agent-based execution; the latter tests target selection and physical behavior. Evaluation must relate both to controlled change in the supplied evidence. Table 15 pairs evaluation questions with resources that make the relevant variation possible. The rows concern different dependencies, so their metrics are interpreted within the stated task setting. In particular, the human-data row measures transfer into trained policy weights, whereas contextual tests intervene on teaching or retained evidence at deployment. This distinction connects evaluation to the data roles in Figure 14. Object substitution and relation transfer. Task novelty has to be defined at the level of the relation being learned. Task suites make adaptation to held-out tasks measurable [227, 311], but withheld names can combine several kinds of change. New object combinations and task templates probe different generalization in VIMA [100]; the Imitator Game separates changes in demonstrated motion from changes in functional intent [101]. familiar procedure on new body tests realization, whereas new ordering of available actions tests contextual composition. useful transfer claim identifies both the unseen relation and the motor competence available to realize it. Object substitution supplies complementary test to changing the demonstrated requirement. Following Table 6, retain the requirement while replacing only the manipulated object, only the receiving object, and then both. Within each condition, compare the correct demonstration, no demonstration, and demonstration specifying another feasible behavior in the same scene. Comparing object conditions measures substitution In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications scope; comparing demonstration conditions measures dependence on teaching. To isolate the demonstration's contribution, keep the instruction fixed or hold its task information constant. Report task interpretation and physical completion separately, verifying the latter through robot execution. The choice of substitutions determines which transfer capability is tested. FUNCTO distinguishes instance and category changes [172], whereas object-pair transfer exposes changes at both ends of relation [347]. Functionally compatible substitutes with different appearances, paired with visually similar but incompatible distractors, can test whether correspondence follows the taught interaction. Training exposure, demonstration count, human correspondence or segmentation assistance, neural updates, and retry opportunities affect the interpretation of this comparison. Undisclosed pretraining leaves training novelty uncertain even when context dependence is established. Withholding relation while preserving familiar objects and executable actions isolates relation novelty; substituting objects while retaining the relation tests its physical transfer. Cross-robot imitation and paired human-video interfaces then extend the change to embodiment and observation [12, 312]. Whether the demonstration remains available is further axis: executing with supplied reference and retaining its lesson after that reference is removed are evaluated separately in Section 7.2. Capture conditions also affect the transfer axis. RoboReel links 2,000 human recordings from four views to simulated trajectories in ten environments, separating clean and distracted recordings from evaluation-only distraction and pose-defined tasks [312]. These variations test whether the same demonstrated requirement survives changed observation interface. Reporting the neural update rule alongside these variations identifies whether transfer uses context or task-specific policy fitting. The real-to-sim benchmark H2RBench tests how human demonstrations support policy training [366]. It reconstructs four real manipulation tasks in simulation, varies human-video quantity at fixed robotdemonstration budget, and compares relative simulation and real-robot performance. Its shared training protocol tests human-data transfer; frozen-policy context interventions test whether newly supplied example changes execution. Both matter when system combines human-video pretraining with contextual adaptation. Navigation across goals and environments. The four context types in Table 13 require different interventions. Changing route demonstration while keeping its destination fixed tests adherence to the taught path or landmark order. Replacing scene preview and clearing memory between goals test spatial evidence and within-environment reuse, respectively; NOLOs context-removal experiment [351] and ReLICs cross-episode attention comparison [203] examine these contributions. Changing instructiondecision examples while retaining the current query tests the demonstrated interpretation. Removing failure notes while retaining backtracking tests whether remembered outcome changes later decisions, as in HAM-VLNs reflection ablation [362]. new building then tests acquisition after environment-specific locations cease to apply. Success weighted by path length (SPL) combines reaching the goal with route efficiency [354]; prescribed route additionally requires an adherence measure, since shortcut can reach the same destination. Success across successive goals measures environment reuse, while repeated wrong turns and stopping errors expose the contribution of feedback. Goal visibility, stopping distance, action discretization, and access to maps or localization define the comparison. Terrain adaptation adds physical cost: VLM-GroNav [353] reports trajectory length and IMU energy density alongside success. Exploration and retries spent acquiring context must be included when relating these gains to total interaction. Simulation, physical navigation, and recorded-scene decisions provide different evidence about execution. NOLOs unseen-layout transfer is evaluated in simulation; its real maze uses separate training and context recordings from that maze. Select2Plan [352] combines simulated object navigation with waypoint assessment on recorded rover scenes, whereas LM-Nav [359] executes routes on physical mobile robot. HAM-VLNs reported comparisons use 100-episode subsets of unseen simulation splits. Together, these settings span simulated transfer, recorded-scene decisions, and physical route execution. Instruction adherence needs alternatives that the scene alone cannot resolve. RoboFollow pairs shared scenes with several feasible behaviors and separates stage-level intent from execution scores [399]. Its layout and semantic recombination tests distinguish choosing the requested object or procedure from physically completing 64 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications it. This provides an operational counterpart to the context interventions above: if only one behavior is plausible in scene, high success can conceal weak use of teaching. RoboFollow tests instruction grounding. Testing unfamiliar rule learning requires held-out rule family and examples that distinguish its candidate rules. Evidence quantity, retention, and distractors. The amount of teaching evidence, retention distance, and distractor load test different properties. LMAct varies the number of expert episodes and includes replay controls, showing that more examples often provide little benefit to the tested models [102]. flat curve can reflect early saturation, weak context use, or inadequate control. Comparing an ambiguous task with fully specified version helps distinguish these causes. Memory benchmarks make the missing evidence more explicit through object, spatial, sequential, or imitation demands [103, 313]. The necessary history depends on the hidden information: AMAGO reports MetaWorld setting whose task can be identified from short history [202]. Checkpoint-based evaluation localizes memory failures. MEMOBench distinguishes Storage, Update, and Compression demands across 30 history-dependent tasks [104]. These test whether decisive events survive retention, revision, and compression. Supplying missing decisive record directly at the policy input, in its expected format, can help distinguish storage or retrieval failure from failure to use available evidence. Intermediate interventions then test physical realization (Section 7.3). WorldLines extends state validity to household traces: Memory QA and downstream planning probe test whether remembered state changes support current answers and action preconditions [375]. EvoEmpirBench isolates dynamic spatial reasoning in locally observable mazes and match-2 games; Agent-ExpVer distills and revises experience across tasks [374]. These settings separate state recall and revision from physical execution, complementing robot rollouts with more targeted memory tests.

sections.title: 7.2 Sources of improvement and comparable evidence
sections.content: Fourteen reported comparisons  (Table 16)  connect context use, physical transfer, and later learning to observable outcomes. Their findings motivate controls that attribute gains to supplied evidence, parameter updates, or retained artifacts. What reported comparisons establish. The first group shows why evidence quantity and usefulness must be separated. ICRTs training-data comparison links context use to task alternatives within scene; LMAct shows that adding expert episodes alone often yields little benefit [13, 102]. BPPs drawing comparison favors demonstrations that specify trajectory, whereas Show-Harnesss action-convention comparison exposes information needed to ground unfamiliar commands [31, 54]. NOLO's context-removal comparison extends this analysis to scene previews [351]. Together, these results connect improvement to the information supplied by context. The second group connects transfer to the execution interface. MT3s low-demonstration advantage relies on alignment followed by interaction replay [36]; part-wise warping improves the tested transfers with supplied part correspondence [347]. Demo-JEPAs comparison with an action head shows that the preferred realization can change with task familiarity [22]. RAPIDs scene-variant ablation adds complementary question: whether the acquired program is verified beyond the demonstrated configuration [390]. Transfer therefore depends jointly on the represented relation, correspondence assistance, motor competence, and conditions used to validate the result. The third group distinguishes using retained experience from acquiring better learner. Zeva tests access to earlier interaction; RTCF and TraceFlow test action correction from successful or failed traces; FARE tests selective revision of the history conditioning prediction [88, 195, 392, 402]. Their scope differs: TraceFlows ordering gains coexist with unresolved simulation deficits, while FAREs always-search variant underperforms its base policy.
