sections.title: 7.3 Physical realization and learning across attempts
sections.content: Channel and intermediate interventions trace contextual information into physical outcomes. Independent physical and memory resets then test whether retained evidence improves later attempts and recovery. Channel interventions complement memory resets. With the task, checkpoint, and recorded history matched, removing language, visual, proprioceptive, or contact inputs tests which evidence supports adaptation. The comparison must retain the policys valid input format and distinguish missing measurement from measured zero. Goal completion and demonstration adherence should also be reported separately when contact is specified: handle-grasp requirement calls for both successful transport and preservation of handle contact. Intermediate interventions localize failure along the four control interfaces. For contextual policy, supply the relevant demonstration segment; for geometric transfer, supply the correct correspondence and reference; for 68 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications predictive control, supply task-consistent future; for an agent, supply the correct executable specification. Each intervention must preserve the controllers expected format. Recovery after the substitution locates bottleneck in the replaced stage or its input. Failure in both conditions calls for tests of downstream execution and interface compatibility. The contrast is most informative at the earliest decision where inferred and required behavior diverge. Target-selection assessment and restored-precondition tests provide related diagnostics [109, 110]. Both conditions require measuring prescribed paths, order, or contacts alongside the terminal state. Physical adaptation requires evidence about the changed condition. MemMimic distinguishes event recall from adaptation to initially unknown physical response, while PACE-Bench varies physical conditions with stable goal and interface [105, 308]. For synthesized teaching videos, the video-generation benchmark H2R-Bench evaluates goal, event, contact, and embodiment consistency before robot execution [314]. These tests are useful when tied to the specific information that the contextual policy must recover. Probe-then-commit audits further separate whether belief covers the action-relevant truth from whether the executor predicts failure accurately [412]. Their offline ground-truth checks show why sharper beliefs alone need not justify physical commitment. Independent physical and memory resets separate the sources of improvement across attempts. Resetting the scene removes task progress, whereas resetting memory removes acquired evidence. Retaining each separately distinguishes physical continuation, contextual adaptation, and additional chances from repeated execution. For trial-memory adaptation, the reuse gain at attempt is reuse . Here Sn is the same predefined success or adherence rate at attempt n; the superscripts keep and reset specify retained and cleared memory. Their difference reuse measures the benefit of retaining evidence from earlier attempts. The comparison holds task distribution, physical initialization, executor, other retained artifacts, earlier attempt count, and execution budget constant; only access to evidence from those attempts changes. Per-attempt rates isolate the benefit of retained evidence, whereas cumulative success also benefits from independent retries. subsequent tool or dynamics change tests whether the learner revises lesson whose physical conditions have become obsolete. Sreset = Skeep n Recovery evaluation connects the detected failure to the acquired evidence, the revised decision, and the outcome of that revision. End-to-end success includes all attempted tasks; conditional repair success concerns the subset of detected, eligible failures. Distinguishing autonomous repair, human correction, and external reset makes their respective contributions visible. Later attempts establish whether the correction remains useful, while newly taught valid procedures test whether the failure detector follows the current task reference. Section 5 describes the corresponding mechanisms. RoboRecover makes the starting deviation reproducible by replaying action prefixes, then evaluating continuation under the original goal [400]. Its 2,000 scenarios distinguish the stage to resume from the deviation to correct, across RoboTwin and LIBERO. Initializing candidate policy history at the recovery point isolates continuation from the reconstructed off-nominal state. contextual-recovery extension should compare retained and cleared prefixes at that same reconstructed state, preserving the continuation budget. This connects reproducible physical deviations to the selective memory resets above.

sections.title: 7.4 Teaching effort, response delay, and reuse cost
sections.content: Contextual adaptation has three operational timescales: acquiring the task, responding to fresh evidence, and reusing the result. Task acquisition includes instruction preparation, demonstration recording, exploration, and validation. Extra search can improve execution with unchanged task information; varying relevant context independently of search budget identifies the contribution of learning [315, 316]. SAILs reconstruction and simulated trials illustrate preparation costs beyond model inference [317]. Acquisition is measured end to end by changeover time: the interval from receiving specification to satisfying stated quality and operating criterion. common criterion permits comparison of contextual teaching, fine-tuning, trajectory reuse, and programming. Elapsed time, human labor, robot interaction, and resets capture different costs: ENPIREs program refinement requires physical trials and verification even with 69 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications fixed neural weights [89]. Repeatable task performance therefore provides more informative endpoint for changeover than first successful attempt. During execution, the relevant delay runs from informative feedback to the affected command. Model inference time, command rate, and servo frequency describe different parts of this interval. Cached demonstration features can be reused, while new contact observation must reach control before the corresponding motion is committed. SimpleMemVLA reports latency falling from 1.02 to 0.68 seconds with identical outputs through scheduling and shared-prefix processing [45]. This scheduling gain reduces response delay while preserving the decision itself. State-dependent steering tests such as ReSteer make the arrival point of feedback explicit [108]. Repeated batches test whether acquisition costs are repaid. Accepted output and intervention time across repeated tasks quantify this return; changing tool or requirement then reveals the cost of obsolete knowledge. These outcomes motivate the next chapter: broader contextual learning must expand what an episode can teach while preserving the ability to revise what no longer applies. Takeaways ① Context interventions establish dependence on task-defining evidence beyond familiar-scene recognition. Physical execution and held-out relation tests then establish how far that requirement transfers. ② Common task outcomes expose the contributions of training, supplied context, adaptive neural state, and retained knowledge. Acquisition and reuse carry different resource costs. ③ Teaching effort, feedback-to-action delay, and cost per accepted execution connect contextual learning to deployment value across repeated attempts.

sections.title: 8 Future Directions: What Limits Transfer and Improvement?
sections.content: Broader contextual learning has four connected objectives: infer unfamiliar rules, preserve binding physical constraints through abstraction, revise retained corrections when conditions change, and improve how subsequent tasks are learned. The directions below connect these objectives to training, representation, and experience acquisition, with behavioral tests that distinguish progress on each.

sections.title: 8.1 From context dependence to a reusable learning rule
sections.content: The learning distinctions introduced in Section 2.1 separate familiar-task selection, composition, and inference of an unfamiliar rule. Building on the learning mechanisms in Section 4.4, we ask which training relationships would extend this behavior to unfamiliar requirements. Table 18 Proposed tests of behavioral transfer in placement task. Keep available objects and motor actions matched; vary what teaching must supply. Novelty is relative to the controlled training exposure. Learning claim What is already familiar What the example must establish Familiar-task selection Object-to-location assignments Choose known leftor right-bin routine Compositional transfer Placement relations; order constraints Combine familiar color and order rules Rule inference Objects; executable placements Infer an unfamiliar size-to-slot rule Table 18 distinguishes selecting familiar task, composing known relations, and inferring new rule. An example can identify routine without teaching new relation: demonstration benefits under incorrect labels in some NLP settings expose the role of task-format recognition [320]. Conversely, function-learning studies show inference of unseen functions, and controlled regression connects task diversity to more general learning behavior [253, 321]. The illustrative robotic tests keep available objects and motor skills fixed while varying what teaching must establish: familiar bin choice, new composition of known constraints, or size-to-slot mapping from family excluded during training. Rule inference requires enough examples to distinguish the candidate mappings. BPPs continuous drawing tasks and the Imitator Games functional substitutions provide concrete task variations from which to design these tests [54, 101]. 70 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications Figure 24 Four research directions: (a) infer taught relations, (b) compose task steps, (c) preserve function across physical changes, and (d) use corrective feedback. Together they extend contextual learning toward interpreting, transferring, and retaining task requirements. The acquisition routes in Section 4.4 motivate testable hypothesis: coverage of task relations and coverage of executable motions make distinct contributions to contextual transfer. Broad pretraining may support unfamiliar requirements, while grounded pairs establish precise action correspondence. Varying pretraining scale and explicit pairing independently, with the executor and task information fixed, would test their contributions. Motion coverage, relation diversity, interaction experience, and model size are distinct factors; agentic systems also expose library size and acquisition cost [53]. Relation-level outcomes and continuous errors are needed alongside all-steps success, because thresholded metrics can make smooth component gains appear abrupt [323]. Cross-modal transfer supplies complementary test. GPT-Policy provides concrete interface in which general VLM receives teaching and acts through fixed robot tools [94]. Expressing the same unfamiliar rule through text, demonstrations, or both would test whether its inferred meaning transfers across formats. Matching task information and motor capabilities isolates rule inference from access to additional details, such as procedural step visible in one format but absent from another. The task examples in Figure 24 connect these research questions to observable behavior. Panel (a) asks whether taught relation determines actions in new scene; (b) extends it to sequence of dependent steps; (c) changes the contact geometry while preserving the interactions function; and (d) uses human feedback to revise the next action. The following sections develop the corresponding teaching, transfer, and retention requirements. Section 8.5 then considers whether experience improves how subsequent requirements are learned.

sections.title: 8.2 Instruction tuning for more complex contextual learning
sections.content: MetaICL and Flan provide language-model precedents for example-based learning and instruction tuning [113, 324]. For ICL for robots, the training problem is to make new teaching select among feasible continuations within controlled motor repertoire. The three cases below progress from combining requirements to revising them and resolving missing information. Figure 25 illustrates these cases through separate kitting episodes with comparable parts and motor skills. Paired, continuous, and corrective records (Section 4.2) provide possible training formats; the intermediate tray states reveal which requirements survive execution. Requirement binding and composition. Panel (a) combines demonstrated plate-first order with request for two plates and three bushings. Reversing the demonstrated order should reverse intermediate tray states while preserving the final inventory. The example separates compositional complexity, which varies skill order and dependencies, from constraint complexity, which adds jointly binding counts, contacts, or dwell times. Measuring each requirement and their joint satisfaction tests whether new composition was followed through the methods intermediate representation. 71 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications Figure 25 Illustrative kitting tasks for three contextual learning problems: (a) combine demonstrated order with requested quantities, (b) change the destination while retaining the order, and (c) resolve an ambiguous destination before acting. Intermediate tray states reveal adherence to teaching beyond the final inventory. Selective revision of procedure. Panel (b) changes the destination to tray before placement, retaining the order and quantities. DROCs language guidance, RACERs corrective supervision, and RoboTTTs separation of failed context from corrective targets offer components for learning such revisions [10, 46, 87]. Training should reward the targeted change together with unaffected requirements. Varying correction timing, scope, and precedence then tests revision complexity: reaching tray while losing the taught count is an overbroad revision. Intervening tasks test whether the revised procedure remains available later. Decision-directed information acquisition. Panel (c) leaves both trays feasible without specifying which to use. Asking for the destination resolves this ambiguity before placement, building on question-based teaching and uncertainty-aware assistance [86, 301]. The acquired answer must preserve the already taught order and quantity. Other uncertainties call for different interventions: view or probe can reveal execution conditions (Section 5), whereas missing grasp skill requires an additional controller or motor learning. Behavioral Exploration offers related action-based route: policy uses interaction history to select expert-like behaviors that explore beyond previous attempts [333]. Clarification and exploration target different unknowns; training should connect each request or action to the information it supplies. These cases motivate comparing action pretraining, demonstration-conditioned training, and mixed instruction demonstrationcorrection training under common backbone and experience budget. Withheld compositions and corrections test requirement adherence, physical completion, and later reuse. The next section examines which requirements should remain invariant when objects and execution conditions change.

sections.title: 8.3 Preserving taught relations across physical change
sections.content: Cross-object transfer in Section 3.5 establishes useful relations when the corresponding parts and admissible substitutions can be identified. The remaining challenge is to infer which demonstrated details are binding and when no valid substitute exists. handleless vessel may serve pouring goal but cannot preserve an 72 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications explicitly required handle grasp. Similarly, pause that lets adhesive set is part of the process, whereas an incidental pause may be shortened. These cases require selective invariance: retain the taught requirement while changing only details that its meaning permits. The part-decomposition study supplies cross-category part equivalencies [347]; learning to infer and validate such equivalencies would extend its transfer scope. The crossed comparisons in Section 7.1 locate these limits by separating changed requirements from changed objects. Beyond successful substitution, learner must recognize when the available objects cannot satisfy the demonstrated relation and acquire the missing information. Contrasting demonstrations or clarification can establish whether pause or contact is required; interaction can reveal whether geometrically compatible replacement has unfamiliar resistance or dynamics [40, 88]. Correspondence and physical feedback therefore answer different questions: where an interaction should occur, and whether that interaction realizes the intended effect. The available executor sets the boundary of this transfer. If the revised requirement can be expressed through existing actions or skills, contextual inference can select new realization. If the necessary motion lies outside that repertoire, further motor learning contributes separate stage, as in human-video-initialized WHIRL [150]. Such hybrid process can preserve context-inferred task relation while learning its physical realization. Navigation introduces related separation between reusable strategy and local knowledge. An exploration strategy can transfer across buildings, while remembered object location is tied to one layout. ReLIC [203] illustrates the value of retaining such local experience across goals. Broader transfer requires identifying which spatial facts remain valid when the environment changes, alongside preserving the task relations considered above.

sections.title: 8.4 Retaining teaching while revising obsolete experience
sections.content: Figure 26 Illustrative reuse of corrective context: (a) an order error, (b) plate-first feedback, and (c) execution in new layout with fixed policy weights. The intermediate tray makes retention of the taught order observable before the kit is complete. Physical transfer preserves requirement across changes in its realization; temporal reuse must also accommodate new teaching. Video outlines and lower-cost planning latents retain different details [31, 325]. later correction can make an initially incidental contact or pause decisive, after task-specific summary has discarded it. Delayed corrections can test what new teaching compact summaries and retrievable source segments support at matched storage and access costs. Preserving current task meaning and enabling future reinterpretation impose different requirements on retained evidence. Consolidation into weights adds training after contextual acquisition. The π0.7 coaching example and the RECAP training framework for π 0.6 connect interaction or correction to subsequent training [273, 281]. Immediate context-driven behavior and persistence after consolidation or reset characterize different stages of acquisition. Retained programs, records, or policy weights can help later tasks, but obsolete corrections can also interfere with new teaching. taught requirement can remain useful after the scene that elicited it has changed. In the kitting example, retained plate-first feedback supplies information absent from the new layout, illustrating how fixed policy could combine an earlier correction with current geometry (Figure 26). Keeping, omitting, or replacing that 73 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications correction tests whether the later decision depends on the acquired lesson. Retention must also survive the representation changes used to make such lessons cheaper to store and apply. Across successive deployments, the criterion also applies to model upgrades and changing environments [127]. Replacing the interpreter or action interface raises two questions: whether retained teaching still governs behavior, and whether revised requirements can override it. An intervening task can leave the earlier procedure available for later reuse; new instruction for that procedure can supersede it. Section 7.4 connects this selective retention to reduced teaching and validation effort.

sections.title: 8.5 Physical recursive self-improvement
sections.content: Physical feedback can improve the current solution or the process used to acquire future solutions. Retained context, program revision, and neural updates provide different means of doing so, with their learning benefit determined by what the successor acquires from new experience. Improved teachability connects these updates to the choice of experience and the cost of acquiring the next task. In the surveys six-horizon framework, S5 names this subsequent-learning objective and S6 extends it to knowledge exchanged between robots. Table 19 Feedback-driven improvement through update target, operation, and reusable output. Targets can overlap; successor comparisons measure their contribution to subsequent learning. ENPIRE and REVOLVE denote their program and policy branches, respectively. Update target Operation Reusable output Examples Interaction context Retain Actioneffect memory RopeFormer [364]; Zeva-Ego [363] Executable artifacts Revise Skills; programs RoboRSI [348]; ENPIRE [89]; HarnessPAI [398] Neural components Fit; retrain Dynamics; policy MetaPusher [368]; REVOLVE [345] Acquisition process Refine Teaching; training procedure LMPC [117]; Eureka [115]; DrEureka [116] Table 19 separates where experience is stored from how it changes subsequent learning. RopeFormer and Zeva-Ego use retained actionresponse history to adapt fixed policy to encountered conditions [363, 364]. Programs retain executable solutions, and neural updates change predictive or motor competence. Any of these can contribute to physical recursive self-improvement when experience improves acquisition or verification on subsequent tasks [326]. The decisive comparison is the later learning process, not the storage format of the change. Program improvement can supply data for subsequent model improvement. HarnessPAI uses validated program rollouts to fine-tune the action model; its published sequence ends at policy refinement, before further round of harness evolution around the improved checkpoint [398]. TraceFlow instead grows an external trace bank with weights fixed, and its reported stacking gains peak before the final round [392]. These examples motivate measuring the successors acquisition rate on new tasks and the persistence of gains across rounds, beyond demonstrating stronger current solver. Learning to become more teachable. LMPC links accumulated teaching to improved subsequent acquisition [117]. Within session, fixed language model converts instructions and corrections into reward code for model-predictive control. Across sessions, successful interactions train it to predict teaching exchanges; the rollout variant searches those exchanges for shorter route to success. Test-task success rises from 39.4% to 66.3%, while mean turns in successful sessions fall from 2.4 to 1.9. This connects experience to successors response to new teaching. For action policies and VLM agents, the corresponding comparison holds new tasks, motor interfaces, and interaction budgets fixed. Evaluating each successor with and without informative context separates improved use of teaching from stronger prior execution. Familiar tasks and fully specified targets measure execution competence; withheld requirements and matched teaching measure acquisition. This extends the controls in Section 7.2 across successive versions of learner. 74 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications Improving execution, supervision, and acquisition. Retained guidance and context-building code can improve selection or interpretation of future evidence [47, 49]. Autonomous practice can improve resetting, execution, or successor policy [114, 141]. RoboRSIs successive skill revisions exemplify repertoire growth; its release-level cumulative coverage records tasks solved at least once [348]. REVOLVE updates two distinct components: failure and correction records retrain the manipulation policy, while mismatch memory refines the supervising agents judgments [345]. Selective resets and successor comparisons attribute gains to the retained solution, control, or supervision. Predictive components offer further update locations. Q-Planning trains value function on deployment experience while retaining the action policy [208]; SILVR trains visual planner on its executions [327]; joint refinement changes both policies and the models that assess or train them [328330]. These loops improve the control and training signals available to contextual learning. Their contribution to teachability is measured by how the resulting successor responds to new evidence, alongside its execution success. Changing the acquisition procedure makes the recursive objective explicit. Eureka revises reward code from policy-training feedback; DrEureka also configures domain randomization for transfer [115, 116]. ENPIRE extends agent-directed experimentation to physical environments, revising programs, data use, and learning algorithms through established interfaces [89]. Retaining effective learning choices together with their applicable conditions offers route to improving future acquisition. Successor comparisons measure this benefit alongside repertoire growth. Evidence from simulated practice and physical experiments characterizes the operating conditions of this improvement. Making the next experience informative. An improving learner can also change what it asks, observes, or tests. EnvGen, OMNI-EPIC, and SimWorld Studio use learner performance to shape subsequent simulated experience [261, 331, 332]. For ICL, teachingexecution pairs near interpretation failures could target conflicting examples, unfamiliar compositions, or corrections with limited scope. Physical trials then test whether the inferred requirement survives contact and embodiment changes. failed insertion makes the distinction concrete. An ambiguous target calls for clarification; an uncertain contact response calls for diagnostic motion. Retaining when each intervention resolved uncertainty could reduce unnecessary demonstrations and trials on later assemblies. The improvement loop then links requirement inference, evidence acquisition, physical verification, and reuse of an acquisition strategy. Collective knowledge evolution. S6 extends the learning cycle to exchanges between robots (Figure 1). An arm can demonstrate placement relation, humanoid realize it under different kinematic constraints, and the receiver return verified execution or correction. The exchanged lesson preserves task order and object relations while allowing grasps and balance control to change. Shared progress and skill representations preserve task content across appearances [29, 30, 79]; multi-robot training supplies compatible competence [57, 132]; morphology interpolation and kinematic constraints support physical realization [131, 133]. Collective knowledge evolution adds reciprocal loop: each execution helps revise knowledge another robot can use. Measuring transfer in both directions, with the teaching and practice required by each body, tests whether the exchange improves the groups subsequent learning. Across individual and collective learning cycles, requirement adherence, correction efficiency, and transfer measure the benefit to subsequent acquisition. Interaction, intervention, and training costs measure the investment required to obtain it. Takeaways ① Diversity in what examples teach, motion coverage, and model scale address different limits. Learning unfamiliar combinations and relation families requires more than recognizing new instances. ② Composition, selective correction, and information acquisition expand what an episode can teach over an available motor repertoire. ③ Retained corrections should change later decisions through context and remain applicable when layouts change. Across longer learning cycles, the central outcome is successor that learns more effectively from new teaching. 75 In-Context Learning for Robots: Methods and Applications

sections.title: 9 Conclusion
sections.content: ICL for robots addresses gap between possessing reusable competence and knowing how to apply it in the present task. Teaching and interaction resolve that gap with deployed neural parameters fixed. Four interfaces carry this information into action: contextual action inference, geometric reference transfer, prediction of consequences, and skill or program execution. Their benefits depend on compatible representations, applicable interaction geometry, realizable predictions, and sufficient executor capabilities, respectively. Correspondence and memory connect the evidence across situations and time; grounding establishes whether it remains usable. The central synthesis is that contextual learning depends on preserving task-relevant distinctions from evidence to execution. Loss during selection, interpretation, realization, or reuse calls for different data, representations, or control capabilities. Across manipulation and navigation, the corresponding tests ask whether changed teaching appropriately redirects behavior, its requirement survives physical change, and retained experience helps later attempts. Acquisition costs and motor competence determine the value and scope of these gains. The next challenge is to make these dependencies transferable: infer unfamiliar combinations of requirements, revise only the constraints affected by feedback, and discard experience whose conditions no longer hold. Physical recursive self-improvement extends this agenda to successor that acquires new tasks more effectively; collective knowledge evolution asks whether verified exchanges improve learning across embodiments. Both are assessed by what later learners acquire and the total teaching, interaction, and training effort required. Image attribution.
